#10348. Quantum computers are getting too powerful to check. Scientists have a solution

As quantum computers grow more powerful, researchers face a troubling question: How can they know whether the results are correct when conventional computers can no longer verify them? Scientists have now developed a promising new method that could help overcome this challenge by measuring the accuracy of quantum simulations and identifying how much uncertainty their predictions contain.

The technique uses experimental measurements to reconstruct how a quantum system behaves, then calculates how uncertainties in that reconstruction affect the results. Researchers successfully demonstrated the approach using a quantum simulator with up to 51 qubits in Innsbruck, Austria.

Quantum systems are expected to become capable of solving increasingly complex problems that traditional computers struggle with or cannot handle at all. However, this progress creates a verification problem. When a simulation is small enough, scientists can compare its results with calculations performed on a conventional computer. As quantum systems grow beyond those limits, that direct comparison becomes impractical, making alternative ways to assess their reliability essential.

A New Way to Measure Quantum Computing Accuracy

The breakthrough comes from an international research team led by Tristan Kraft at the Technical University of Munich and Peter Zoller at the University of Innsbruck and the Institute for Quantum Optics and Quantum Information of the Austrian Academy of Sciences, working alongside Barbara Kraus of the Technical University of Munich. The researchers developed a method for experimentally determining how a quantum simulator operates and translating uncertainties in its behavior into measurable limits on the accuracy of its results.

Quantum simulators are specialized physical systems designed to reproduce the behavior of other quantum systems. They are especially useful for investigating situations involving large numbers of interacting particles, where the calculations required can quickly overwhelm even powerful conventional computers.

But quantum experiments are never entirely free from errors. "But no real experiment is perfect," says Tristan Kraft. "Interactions may turn out differently than expected, the system is influenced by its environment, and measurements are also subject to uncertainties."

Rather than assuming a quantum simulator behaves exactly as intended, the new approach examines experimental data to determine what is actually happening inside the system. This allows researchers to identify important interactions and account for disturbances such as fluctuations and noise.

"From this data, we determine the relevant interactions as well as key influences from fluctuations and noise. We then calculate how the uncertainties in this model affect the simulation results," explains Tristan Kraft. "The quantum simulator thus provides not just a single value, but a result with error margins that quantify its accuracy."

Successfully Tested on a 51 Qubit Quantum Simulator

To evaluate the method, the researchers began with a relatively small quantum system containing ten trapped ions. Because conventional computers can still calculate the behavior of a system of this size, the team could test its reconstructed models and calculated error limits against independent measurements.

After this initial validation, the researchers expanded their experiments to a chain of 51 trapped ions. The larger demonstration, carried out by a team led by Manoj Joshi and Christian Roos using an ion trap quantum simulator, showed that the technique could also work with substantially more complex quantum systems.

This represents an important step toward establishing how trustworthy quantum simulation results are, particularly as quantum devices advance into territory where direct verification with traditional computing methods becomes increasingly difficult.

Extending the Breakthrough to More Complex Quantum Systems

The next challenge is to bring the technique to two-dimensional quantum simulators. These systems can model more complicated interactions among particles, making them valuable for exploring quantum physics. At the same time, their growing complexity makes their results particularly difficult to confirm using conventional calculations.

"This is particularly important because classical calculations for such systems become significantly more difficult as the number of particles increases," explains quantum computing pioneer Peter Zoller. "This also makes independent verification of the results increasingly complex, making the question of experimentally determined error limits all the more important."

The researchers are now adapting their method for the newest generation of two-dimensional quantum simulators, which offer improved precision and can investigate systems containing larger numbers of particles.

Looking further ahead, the approach could help scientists establish a more meaningful way to measure quantum advantage, the ability of quantum systems to outperform conventional computers. Instead of comparing machines based only on their processing speed or the size of the problems they can handle, researchers could also examine how accurately each system produces its answers.

"After all, when a classical computer and a quantum simulator tackle the same problem, it's not just a matter of which one delivers a result faster. What's also crucial is which one can solve the problem with a smaller, verifiable margin of error," says Peter Zoller.

This shift could change how progress in quantum computing is evaluated. Future breakthroughs may be judged not simply by how many particles a simulator can model or how quickly it performs calculations, but by its ability to solve increasingly difficult problems with demonstrably reliable results.

The findings were published in Physical Review X. The research received support from the Austrian Science Fund (FWF), the German Ministry of Research, Technology and Space, the European Union, BMW, and other funding organizations.

#10342. How to Migrate an Elementor Site to the WordPress Block Editor

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Elementor made your site easy to build. It may also be making it slow. Here's how to move a site onto the Block Editor without breaking URLs, losing content or dropping out of Google.

Page builders solved a real problem. Before the Block Editor matured, they were the easiest way to give clients drag-and-drop layouts. Many of those sites are still running today, and a lot of them are slow on phones.

The data backs that up. According to the HTTP Archive Core Web Vitals Technology Report for June 2026, 36.8% of Elementor sites pass Core Web Vitals on mobile. Sites built with the Block Editor pass 53.0% of the time. That's correlation, not proof, since hosting and setup matter too. But in my experience, it matches what happens when you remove the builder from a slow site.

My reason for migrating sites off Elementor is simple: **page builders make websites heavy. **Having said that, Elementor has improved a lot. Its performance settings, Flexbox Containers, and asset-loading options cut much of the bloat, and a carefully tuned Elementor site can pass Core Web Vitals. But tuning only goes so far. You’re still shipping the builder’s framework, wrapper markup and scripts, and every plugin or Elementor update is a chance for the speed to slip again.

For small business sites that don’t need drag-and-drop editing, rebuilding the same design on the WordPress Block Editor (Gutenberg) removes that weight at the source, without changing what the client sees.

This guide follows the order I use. It assumes you're comfortable with WordPress admin, WP-CLI and a staging site. If you need to set those up first, SitePoint's guide to the ultimate WordPress development environment covers the tooling.

Not every Elementor site needs to move. Migration makes sense when:

It's harder to justify when the site leans on Elementor Pro features you'd need to replace, such as complex popups, dynamic loops or WooCommerce templates. Those can all be rebuilt, but the job gets bigger fast.

You can't prove a migration worked without "before" numbers. Capture these on the live site first.

Crawl the site with a tool such as Screaming Frog, and export every indexable URL with its title, meta description, H1 and canonical tag. You can also pull published pages and posts with WP-CLI:

Run Google PageSpeed Insights, which uses Lighthouse for its lab scores, on the homepage and two or three key templates. Save the mobile lab scores and, if the site has enough traffic, the field data from real users.

Export the last three months of pages and queries from Google Search Console. That's what you'll compare against after launch.

Elementor stores each page's layout as JSON in the elementordata post meta field, and marks builder pages with elementoredit_mode. This command lists every page that uses the builder:

Then list everything else Elementor controls, which is easy to miss:

On the small business sites I've migrated, the inventory usually turns up more than the owner expects. The pages are the easy part. The surprises are saved templates nobody remembers creating, a popup still running on every page, add-on widgets from plugins that were installed once and forgotten, and contact forms that live inside Elementor Pro rather than a form plugin. Finding those before the rebuild saves a broken launch.

Work on a staging copy. Install a block theme, such as Twenty Twenty-Five or a lightweight starter theme, and move the Elementor global styles into theme.json. That way colors, fonts and spacing are defined once, instead of in every widget.

Copy the hex values and font names from Elementor's Site Settings so the new site matches the old one. Rebuild the header and footer as template parts in the Site Editor. If you'd rather write a theme yourself, SitePoint's series on building a WordPress theme from scratch covers the basics.

Most Elementor sites repeat the same few sections: a hero, a services grid, testimonials and a call to action. Build each one once as a block pattern, then reuse it on every page. Patterns are plain block markup, so you don't need React to write them, whatever you may have heard about React and WordPress development.

In a block theme, any PHP file in the /patterns folder with a header comment is registered automatically:

For page content, there's a useful shortcut. Elementor saves a plain HTML copy of each page into post_content. Open a page in the Block Editor, and the old content usually appears in a Classic block. Choose Convert to blocks, then delete the leftovers and rebuild the layout with your patterns. It keeps the copy and images, so you only redo the design.

The difference shows up in the page source. Here's typical front-end markup for a single heading on an Elementor page, using the older section and column layout:

Newer Elementor versions with Flexbox containers and the optimized markup settings trim some of those wrappers, but most older sites still carry all of them. Multiply that by every element on every page, and the weight adds up.

To speed up this step, I built a free Elementor to Gutenberg converter. Paste in a page's elementordata JSON from Step 2, and it returns block markup you can paste into the Block Editor's code editor. It handles headings, text, images, buttons, spacers, dividers and column layouts, and lists anything it can't convert, such as forms and popups, for you to rebuild by hand. It runs entirely in your browser, so the page data never leaves your computer.

The code is rarely what holds a migration up. Content is. Once clients see their site being rebuilt, many decide it's time to rewrite their pages too, and the project ends up waiting on copywriters and approvals. My fix is to separate the two: migrate the existing content as it is, launch, then update the copy afterwards. That keeps the speed and SEO gains on schedule, and it means any ranking change can be traced to either the migration or the new copy, not both at once.

This is the step that decides whether rankings hold.

To spot-check a redirect or a status code from the command line:

When staging matches the live site, deploy it. Then:

Leave the old elementordata meta in place for a few weeks, in case you need to roll back. Once you're confident, take a backup and remove it to shrink the database.

Run PageSpeed Insights again straight away for lab scores. Field data takes longer: the Chrome UX Report uses a rolling 28-day window, so give it a month before judging real-user results. Compare Search Console clicks for the same period before and after launch.

In my migrations, the biggest change is usually page weight and loading time, because the builder's CSS, JavaScript and wrapper markup are gone. What doesn't always improve is server response time. If the site is on slow shared hosting, the first byte still arrives late, and that needs a hosting fix, not a rebuild. Search traffic should hold steady if the URLs and metadata were protected. If it drops, the Step 5 crawl comparison is the first place to look.

Moving off Elementor isn't a one-click job, but it isn't a full redesign either. Record a baseline, inventory what the builder controls, rebuild with patterns, and protect every URL. Most of the speed gain comes from removing code the site never needed. For what to tackle after that, see these practical web performance techniques. Most of the risk comes from rushing the SEO checks. Done carefully, the client gets the same site, a faster one, and an editor that comes with WordPress itself.

#10337. Automating Contract Signing in Node.js: Webhooks, Verification, and Storing Signed PDFs

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Sending a document for signature is the easy part of an e-signature integration. One POST request and the signer gets an email. The work that actually breaks in production happens afterwards: knowing when the document was signed, trusting the notification that told you so, handling the same notification twice, and getting the final PDF into storage before the download link expires.

This tutorial builds that whole loop in Node.js with Express. An event in your app (a deal is approved, a client is onboarded, a task moves to "ready to sign") sends a contract from a template. When the signer finishes, a webhook arrives, your server verifies it, and the signed PDF plus its audit trail get saved without anyone touching them.

The code uses Firma.dev, the e-signature API I work on, because I needed a real API to make the examples runnable. The patterns are not specific to it, though. Signature verification, idempotent handlers, short-lived download URLs, and reconciliation jobs show up in almost every webhook-driven integration, and the same structure applies whether you're receiving events from a payment processor, a CI system, or another signing provider.

There's a fifth part that tutorials usually skip: a reconciliation job that catches anything the webhooks missed. We'll build that too, because webhooks are a notification mechanism, not a delivery guarantee.

Before sending anything, wrap the HTTP calls in one place. This is where authentication lives, and it's also where you handle 429 Too Many Requests once instead of in every caller. Most APIs, this one included, return a Retry-After header on a 429, so the client should honour it rather than guessing a backoff.

The 503 branch matters later. When a document has just been completed, the final PDF and its completion certificate take a moment to generate, and the download endpoint says so with a 503 and a Retry-After instead of handing you a half-built file.

The trigger depends on your product. It might be a route handler, a queue consumer, or a CRM automation calling into your service. What matters is that the function doing the sending is small and takes plain data:

Two design choices are worth calling out.

Use a single create-and-send call when you can. Many signing APIs split this into "create a draft" and "send the draft." That's useful when a human needs to review the document first, but for automation it creates a window where your process can crash between the two calls and leave an orphaned draft. A combined endpoint makes the operation atomic from your side.

Store the provider's ID on your own record immediately. Webhook payloads reference the signing request, not your deal or customer. Without that mapping you'll end up searching by email address, which falls apart as soon as one client signs two documents.

Here's the first place integrations quietly go wrong. Webhook signatures are computed over the exact bytes the sender transmitted. If Express parses the body as JSON first, you lose those bytes, and re-serialising the object won't reproduce them (key order, whitespace, and number formatting can all change). Signature checks then fail intermittently, which is the worst kind of failure.

The fix is to use express.raw() on the webhook route only, so the handler receives a Buffer:

Most webhook providers sign payloads with HMAC-SHA256 using a shared secret. The details vary, so read your provider's docs for the exact header format, but the scheme here is common: the header looks like t=1731456000,v1=5f2b..., and the signed string is the timestamp, a dot, and the raw body. Stripe uses a very similar format, and the Standard Webhooks spec describes the same idea as a vendor-neutral convention.

Each line here defends against something specific.

The OWASP guidance on cryptographic storage covers the other half of this: the secret belongs in an environment variable or secrets manager, never in the repository.

Every serious webhook system delivers at least once, not exactly once. If your endpoint is slow, returns a 5xx, or the network drops the response, the sender retries. Firma.dev, for example, makes up to three attempts per event (immediately, then after at least five minutes, then after at least an hour) and treats anything other than a 2xx as a failure, including redirects. Other providers retry more aggressively. Either way, your handler will eventually see the same event twice.

The defence is to record each event's unique ID and skip ones you've seen. In the server above that's alreadyProcessed and markProcessed. For a demo, a Set works:

In production, use your database and let a unique constraint do the work, so two concurrent deliveries can't both pass the check:

Also notice the order in the route: respond with 200, then do the work. Many providers time out deliveries after a few seconds (five, in this case). Downloading a PDF and uploading it to object storage can easily take longer than that, and a timeout counts as a failure, which triggers a retry, which triggers duplicate work. Acknowledging fast and processing asynchronously avoids that loop.

setImmediate is fine for a tutorial, but it has a real weakness: if the process dies after sending the 200 and before finishing the work, the event is acknowledged and lost. In production, push the event onto a durable queue (BullMQ, SQS, a jobs table) before responding. Step 7 covers the safety net for whatever still slips through.

Now the actual business logic. You'll usually see several event types (sent, viewed, a signer signed, declined, expired, completed). Only one of them means "the document is final":

Three things in here are easy to get wrong.

Don't treat "a signer signed" as "the document is done." With multiple signers, each one triggers its own event, and a per-signer "all complete" flag can be true on more than one of them. Key your storage logic off the single completion event.

Don't persist the download URL. Pre-signed URLs expire (this one carries an expires_at). Saving the link to your database and serving it to users later produces broken links a few minutes or hours later. Download the bytes and store them in storage you control. Swapping the fs.writeFile calls for an S3 PutObject or a Google Drive upload is a drop-in change.

Store the audit trail, not just the PDF. If a signature is ever disputed, the PDF shows what was signed, and the audit trail shows who signed it, when, and from where (timestamps, IP addresses, the sequence of views and signatures). That evidence is what makes an electronic signature defensible, which brings us to the legal side.

Retries are finite. Endpoints go down during deploys. Some providers auto-disable a webhook after enough consecutive failures, and events aren't guaranteed to arrive in order. Any one of these can leave a completed document sitting unsaved.

A small scheduled job closes that gap. Keep a list of signing requests your app considers "pending," and periodically ask the API for their real status:

Since storeSignedDocument overwrites by ID, running it twice for the same document is harmless. That's the property you want from every step in a webhook pipeline: doing it again shouldn't change the result.

None of this is legal advice, but a few facts shape how you build.

In the US, the ESIGN Act and the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act (adopted by 49 states) give electronic signatures the same legal standing as handwritten ones for most commercial documents. ESIGN also has requirements around consumer consent and record retention, which is part of why you store the final PDF yourself rather than relying on a third-party link.

In the EU, eIDAS defines three levels: simple (SES), advanced (AdES), and qualified (QES). SES and AdES cover most business contracts. QES requires a qualified trust service provider and certificate-based identity, and some documents (certain property transfers and court filings, depending on the country) require it or exclude e-signatures entirely. Check which level your document types need before you pick a provider, since not every API offers every level.

Across jurisdictions, the evidence that holds up is the same: who signed, how they were identified, when it happened, and proof the document hasn't changed since. That's the audit trail and the completion certificate, which is why Step 6 stores both.

If you're evaluating providers for a workflow like this, the questions that matter at the integration level are mostly not on the pricing page:

The send call is one line. The reliability comes from everything around it: keeping the raw body for verification, checking timestamps and comparing in constant time, acknowledging fast and deduplicating by event ID, downloading files before their links expire, and running a reconciliation job for the events that never arrive. Get those right and contract signing becomes something your app does in the background, with no one chasing signatures or copying PDFs between folders.

For the Firma.dev-specific details used here (event names, header format, rate limits), see the webhooks guide.

#10336. Is the Galaxy S26 Ultra still a good buy at the end of 2026?

Yes, the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra remains a good buy in late 2026 if you want a large-screen Android phone with versatile cameras, an integrated S Pen, and long-term software support.

The Galaxy S26 Ultra has aged very well, benefiting from Samsung’s mature hardware and software, along with a host of other quality-of-life improvements gained from its recent update to One UI 9 running Android 17.

We’re going to take a deeper dive at what the S26 Ultra is, and how it compares to its cheaper siblings, in a quest to figure out whether it’s still worth your time and money this holiday season.

The Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra is the highest-end model in Samsung’s 2026 Galaxy S26 lineup. Released back on March 11, it pairs a 6.9-inch display with a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 processor, a built-in S Pen, and a four-camera system led by a 200MP main sensor.

It’s a powerful device, built for photography enthusiasts and professionals who want to get the most out of their phones while on the go. Its large screen size belies a relatively compact, portable device that’s a pleasure to do work on, from writing emails to taking photos to taking meeting notes using the S Pen.

We also found dependable everyday endurance from the 5,000mAh battery, and now that the phone supports 60-watt wired charging, quick top-ups become more useful. Samsung also promises seven generations of OS upgrades and seven years of security updates from launch, an important consideration if you plan to keep your next phone for several years.

At launch, US pricing started at $899.99 for the Galaxy S26, $1,099.99 for the Galaxy S26+, and $1,299.99 for the Galaxy S26 Ultra, each with 256GB of storage. But those prices have dropped over the past few months, and you may be able to get them for less. We’ve seen the S26 Ultra, for example, as low as $999.99 during Prime Day.

Having different lenses gives you more options for portraits, travel photos, and subjects you can’t easily walk closer to.

The regular Galaxy S26 is the more natural choice if you prioritize a smaller phone and a lower purchase price. The Galaxy S26+ makes sense if you want a large-screen Galaxy without paying for Ultra-specific features.

The biggest improvement since launch is the move from Android 16-based One UI 8.5 to Android 17-based One UI 9.

One UI 9 offers several practical additions. Now Nudge suggestions extend beyond the keyboard into conversation notifications and a floating button. The quick panel offers more customization, and Samsung DeX gains easier movement between desktops and desktop previews in Recents.

Samsung has also made Smart Switch even better, which allows you to quickly and easily port over your apps, data, and media from another device.

The Galaxy S26 Ultra’s features are most useful when they solve problems or make everyday moments feel joyful and seamless. Here are five examples:

If you’re coming from a Galaxy S22 or S23 series phone, there are so many upgrades, small and large, that are awaiting you with the S26 Ultra.

The Galaxy S26 Ultra and Samsung’s other products are on sale during Best Buy’s Holiday Deals event.

GTA V’s original PC release asks for a 1GB card; this one has a sixteenth of that.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

YouTube channel Budget-Builds Official has done the unthinkable, getting Grand Theft Auto V to run on a Radeon graphics card from 2007 with just 64MB of VRAM. The game is almost downright playable, too, with config edits, a move to Windows 8, and an overclock getting its speed up from just 1 FPS into the 13 to 20 FPS range, sans most cars, that is.

The channel detailed the feat, which targets a GPU with just a sixteenth of the video memory that’s usually required to play the game. GTA V Legacy lists, as its minimum, an Nvidia 9800 GT or AMD HD 4870, both cards with DirectX 10 support and 1GB of VRAM. The Enhanced version, released in 2025, needs 4GB, from a GTX 1630 or RX 6400 as specified.

In fact, the chosen card, an ATI Radeon HD 2350, is potentially the worst card that can launch GTA V, at least by the tester’s claim, even though its DDR2 memory is probably one of the few types not in short supply at the moment. Notably, this approach doesn’t involve using a unified or shared system memory AMD APU workaround; this is dedicated VRAM. It’s also not the first attempt at something like this, as the channel has an earlier run with 8MB of VRAM on games like Half-Life 2 and Minecraft.

Reaching the final settings took “the best part of half a day” of tweaking, after which it was possible to complete the prologue and the first mission. In some respects, the end result “genuinely does look like a PS2 game,” which probably wouldn’t actually faze fans of the series. However, for this specific title, the modder believes that “this is as low as you can actually go with GTA V.” Going any lower would likely mean reimagining the game in some way.

The game’s first launch with the card, on Windows 10 and the Catalyst 13.1 driver, led to a start screen hang of about 10 minutes. The game was expecting the previous HD 6900-series card, and a settings deletion plus relaunch got things back into action. One of the video’s chapter titles, “We are in GAME... at 1FPS,” summarizes the experience pretty well.

The plan was to use the lowest in-menu settings, of course, and then the config file from the channel’s earlier 256MB run with various settings: no shadows, no reflections, and a resolution around 240p. This got things to 3 FPS, a significant improvement, but far from good enough. Changes to level-of-detail values to their lowest levels got things up to 10 FPS. However, it wasn’t yet time to give up.

Downgrading to Windows 8 and Catalyst 12.6, “the original display drivers for Windows 8,” as well as an older build of the game, paved the pathway forward. Importantly, the OS exposed overclocking that wasn’t available in Windows 10, so a second fan went onto the card first, and the GPU’s core was pushable from 400MHz to 520MHz with the assistance of MSI Afterburner. Pushing the memory from 400MHz to 475MHz led to a black screen, and the video doesn’t say what the memory ended up at, though the card survived.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

The Windows 8 setup reached 14 FPS, and further engine-file edits, to visual settings.dat and to level-of-detail options through OpenIV, put gameplay in the 13 to 20 FPS range.

Ignore the dots on the screen during gameplay; the tester says these are from being out of memory, verified by an artifact-free Unigine Valley run.

The game ended up playable, although, aside from the dots, it had many other visual issues: gaps between vertices in the world, and side characters had far fewer textures than the main ones. Additionally, most cars didn’t render, since keeping them loaded crashed the game with out-of-memory errors. This makes police “hover” into scenes and, hilariously, pop out of invisible cars. Likewise, the train in the prologue never actually loads. First-person driving, at least, works. All of this plays within that range, although busier city streets can drop from 15 down to 11 or 12 FPS.

The creator says the full gameplay will likely go up as its own video on a second channel, in “lossless quality.” The video is timely, acting as a send-off just before GTA VI’s release on Nov. 19, although not yet on PC, with a PC version reportedly due next year.

#10333. Google Health update fixes my biggest Fitbit Air complaint with ‘in-progress’ workout card

Google’s Fitbit Air is one of my favorite products of 2026 and my preferred workout companion, but not being able to see a workout while you’re in the middle of it has been a huge complaint of mine, and the latest Google Health update is fixing that.

Quite literally at the start of this week, I was on a walk through my neighborhood and though to myself, “it’s still pretty annoying that I can’t see my workout progress in the Google Health app.” It’s been a complaint of mine for a while, as various treadmill sessions and more have left me wondering what my heart rate is looking like, how many steps I’ve taken, etc, and it’s only a problem when using the Fitbit Air, seeing as the Pixel Watch (or Fitbit Edge) I’d wear otherwise will show that data front and center.

In the changelog for Google Health 5.13, Google details a new “exercise in-progress” card on the main “Today” screen. This will show what exercise is being tracked and also let you end the workout early.

If you use your Pixel Watch, Fitbit Air, or Fitbit Edge to automatically track your exercises, you’ll now see an exercise-in-progress card on your mobile app’s Today screen. This card lets you know that your device is tracking your exercise and gives you the opportunity to end the tracking and get your summary whenever you want.

We don’t know exactly what this card looks like just yet, but it sounds like it fits the need perfectly.

Google Health 5.13 is now rolling out on Android and iOS.

She used eye tracking and gyroscopes for thumbstick control.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

EEG machines are used to detect and record brain activity, so one enterprising tech enthusiast decided to use them to play GTA VI. Creator Perri Karyal showed her feat on X, where she streamed her gameplay while wearing a wireless electroencephalogram (EEG) designed for research.

I STOLE A JET WITH MIND CONTROL IN GTA6 this took me AGES you have no idea what should I do next?? This electroencephalogram (EEG) records my brain activity and when I'm imagining something I've trained the software to recognise (like pushing a cube forward), a button will be pressed on my virtual xbox controller. For this run, I was imagining pushing a boulder to accelerate, getting angry to interact with vehicles, and imagining a cricket hopping to jump. I use eyetracking and gyro for joysticks :)November 22, 2026

Perri could be seen jumping a fence with Jason on a motorbike, before proceeding toward a parked fighter to steal and fly it. Her brain activity is overlaid on the screen while she’s playing, and viewers could also see the creator intensely focused on the game.

She trained the software to recognize specific brain signals and mapped them to an action on her Xbox controller. For example, imagining pushing a cube forward would correspond to a button press, getting angry lets her interact with cars and other vehicles, while picturing a hopping cricket would also make her character jump. The joysticks, on the other hand, are controlled via eye tracking and through gyroscopes on the head unit.

While Perri makes it look effortless, using the EEG device for gaming is way harder than what many people think. “People don’t realize how challenging it is!” Karyal replied to a comment. One viewer also mentioned the huge mass of brainwaves that appeared on the screen when she took off on the jet, to which she responded, “I was so stressed out. DO YOU KNOW HOW MANY TIMES I TRIED TO DO THIS.” Even though using wireless EEG for gaming does not have any apparent side effects, the creator said that she gets headaches after hours of gaming because of how much the headset squeezes her head.

This isn’t the first time that we’ve seen people playing games using just their mind. Neuralink has recently shown off one of its patients shooting at NPCs and even “threading the needle” with a speedboat using a brain-computer interface (BCI) chip. The big difference between Perri’s creation and Neuralink’s BCI, though, is that the latter requires invasive neurosurgery.

It may be surprising to think how a tech creator could beat Neuralink at its own game, but the latter has already applied the technology to multiple trial patients. We’ve seen them playing complicated games like World of Warcraft and Counter-Strike 2, while others used it for productivity and creativity, like editing a YouTube video.

These technologies are still in the development and trial phases or are being experimented on by enterprising creators and tech tubers. However, it also gives hope to individuals with limited mobility, as it gives them hope that they could regain some form of mobility and independence in the future.

As spotted by TheHDRoom on Twitter and on the 4K Blu-ray subreddit, Best Buy is now selling 14 different 4K Blu-rays on its website, marking another step in the brand’s slow return to selling physical media. These films include:

Technically, Blu-ray returned to Best Buy’s online storefront in August of 2025, when it opened a third-party marketplace similar to Amazon or Walmart. These titles, however, are shipped and sold by Best Buy. Everything’s still online-only, unfortunately, save for The Odyssey, which launched in-store shelf displays alongside yesterday’s release date. It shouldn’t come as too much of a surprise that The Odyssey is getting some special treatment; in addition to its status as a box office juggernaut, Nolan’s previous movie, Oppenheimer, initially sold out of physical copies in its first week of release in 2023.

Outside of these 14 titles, additional Blu-rays continue to be sold through Best Buy’s third-party marketplace.

Update, 11/20: Best Buy confirmed to The HD Room on Twitter that The Odyssey is just the first 4K Blu-ray to return to physical locations, as it plans to continue adding “some” Blu-rays back to its stores.

Darrell Dai says he's "open to exploring the possibility of returning"

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Former Nvidia robotics engineer Darrell Dai made a viral post just nine days ago announcing his resignation from Nvidia, which has gathered over 7 million impressions on X alone (Dai also posted to his LinkedIn account). Dai resigned due to what he described as a lack of transparency around CEO Jensen Huang's exit. But now that Huang is back at the helm, Dai has followed up, saying that he "may have moved too quickly," although his resignation has already taken effect.

Welcome back, Jensen. I’m happy to see you return, and happy for my friends and former colleagues at NVIDIA. Looking back, I may have moved too quickly, and I don’t want to rush into another major decision. For now, I’d like to take some time to rest, reflect, and think carefully about my future. As part of that, I’m open to exploring the possibility of returning. Thank you for all the kindness and encouragement. Whatever comes next, I want to approach it with a clearer mind and give it the thought it deserves.November 23, 2026

Dai says that although he's open to the possibility of returning to Nvidia, he wants to approach his next decision with "a clearer mind." Huang resigned 11 days ago following reports of two separate affairs, one of which reportedly involved an alleged Chinese intelligence asset.

Despite reports of belligerent behaviors toward employees, Nvidia retains an exceptional rating on Glassdoor, and many employees rallied around the CEO's return. A petition to reinstate Huang gathered over 150,000 signatures online, including high-profile names like Elon Musk.

Huang publicly admitted to having an affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang. In his statement, the Nvidia co-founder apologized to his wife of 41 years, Lori Huang, and his two children, Spencer Huang and Madison Huang, both of whom still work at Nvidia.

Days following the admission, a report from The New York Times accused Huang of having another affair with Nvidia executive Kimberly Powell, who reported directly to Huang, citing five anonymous sources within Nvidia. Huang resigned as CEO the following day. Neither Huang nor Powell have commented on the alleged affair.

Dai's last day at Nvidia was November 19, just a few days ago. President Donald Trump said on Monday that he contacted Nvidia's board, and went as far as to claim he "made the deal," according to CNBC. Following the announcement of Huang's return, Nvidia's stock rose more than 30% upon market open.

#10326. Preventing API Contract Drift in TypeScript Applications

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A frontend application can compile successfully and still fail when it communicates with the backend.

Imagine a backend developer changes an API response from:

The backend works correctly. The frontend also builds without errors. However, a component expecting user.name now receives undefined.

This is an example of API contract drift: the frontend and backend no longer agree on the structure or behavior of an API.

The problem becomes more difficult when several developers or teams work on different parts of an application. A change made by one team may affect another team's assumptions without producing an obvious error during development.

TypeScript helps catch many programming mistakes, but its types do not automatically validate data received over HTTP. A type declaration can describe what the application expects without proving that the server actually returns it.

In this tutorial, we'll look at a practical way to make API contracts more reliable.

Consider a typical frontend API function:

The function promises to return a User, so TypeScript allows the application to access properties such as name and email.

The return value of response.json() is not automatically checked against the User interface. The interface only provides compile-time information; it does not validate the actual JSON received from the server.

the frontend may still treat the response as a User even though the data has a different structure.

This is particularly important when working with:

Independently deployed frontend and backend applications.

APIs maintained by different engineering teams.

The solution is to validate data at the boundary where it enters the application.

Zod is a TypeScript-first schema validation library. It allows developers to describe expected data structures and validate actual values against those definitions.

Now create a schema for the user response:

First, UserSchema describes the structure that the application expects at runtime.

Second, z.infer generates the corresponding TypeScript type from the schema.

This means developers do not need to maintain a separate interface and validation definition for the same data structure.

The response is initially treated as unknown, which prevents the application from assuming that untrusted data already has the expected structure.

UserSchema.parse() validates the actual response.

If the backend returns an unexpected property type or misses a required field, Zod throws a validation error instead of allowing invalid data to move silently through the application.

You can also use safeParse() when you prefer to handle validation errors without exceptions:

This approach is useful when API responses are external or when a frontend must provide more controlled error handling.

One common mistake is placing API validation logic directly inside React components.

For a small application, this may seem convenient. As the project grows, however, it becomes difficult to reuse validation rules and identify where data transformations happen.

A better approach is to separate API schemas, service functions, and UI components.

The responsibilities are straightforward:

schemas/user.ts defines the expected user data.

api/client.ts handles common HTTP configuration.

api/users.ts contains user-related API requests.

hooks/useUser.ts manages data fetching for React.

components/UserProfile.tsx displays the validated data.

This structure makes it easier to change an API implementation without rewriting the UI.

It also makes testing more manageable because validation logic can be tested independently of React rendering.

For more ideas on organizing application code, see SitePoint's guide to modern JavaScript modules.

Runtime validation protects an application when data arrives. However, teams also need a shared description of what an API is supposed to accept and return.

OpenAPI provides a standard format for describing HTTP APIs, including:

For example, an endpoint can be described using an OpenAPI document:

This document describes what the endpoint should return.

Both frontend and backend developers can refer to the same contract instead of relying on separate assumptions or outdated documentation.

Swagger Editor helps developers write and validate OpenAPI documents. It also provides a convenient way to inspect API definitions.

Swagger UI turns an OpenAPI document into interactive API documentation, allowing developers to explore endpoints and test requests.

Redoc provides another way to generate readable API documentation from an OpenAPI specification.

These tools are particularly useful when APIs are maintained by multiple developers or consumed by several applications.

Maintaining API types manually across frontend and backend repositories creates opportunities for inconsistencies.

For example, a backend developer might add a new optional property while the frontend continues using an older interface.

One way to reduce this duplication is to generate TypeScript definitions and API clients from an OpenAPI specification.

Orval is a useful tool for this workflow.

It can generate TypeScript clients and types from an OpenAPI document, helping frontend developers work with consistent endpoint definitions.

A typical configuration might look like this:

The exact configuration depends on the Orval version and the structure of the OpenAPI document.

Once configured, the client can be regenerated when the API specification changes.

This reduces the amount of repetitive code developers need to maintain manually.

However, generated types should not be confused with runtime validation. They improve consistency during development, but an application may still need to validate responses received from external systems or services that cannot be fully trusted.

Frontend developers often need to build or test features before the corresponding backend endpoint is ready.

Waiting for a complete backend implementation can slow down development, particularly when multiple teams work independently.

Mock Service Worker (MSW) helps solve this problem by intercepting network requests and returning controlled responses.

You can define a mock handler for the user endpoint:

The frontend can now make normal HTTP requests while MSW supplies predictable responses during development or testing.

You can also simulate an invalid response:

This makes it possible to check whether the application's validation and error-handling logic behave as expected.

MSW is particularly valuable because it allows frontend tests to run without requiring a live backend environment.

Runtime validation and generated clients improve reliability, but they do not automatically guarantee that independently developed services remain compatible.

For systems with multiple services, contract testing can provide another layer of protection.

Pact is a contract-testing tool that allows consumers and providers to verify their expectations about API interactions.

Consider a frontend application that expects the user endpoint to return:

The consumer defines the expected interaction.

The backend provider can then run verification against that contract to check whether its actual response satisfies the consumer's expectations.

This helps identify breaking changes before they reach production.

These tools solve different problems. A project does not necessarily need all of them, but larger applications can benefit from combining the approaches that match their architecture.

A contract is only useful if developers consistently check it when making changes.

A practical approach is to run validation and tests automatically whenever someone opens a pull request.

For example, a GitHub Actions workflow might look like this:

The api:validate script should be configured to validate the project's OpenAPI document or run the relevant contract checks.

The test command should execute the application's automated tests.

For a production project, you may also want to include:

The objective is to detect incompatible changes before they are merged.

A failed pipeline gives developers an opportunity to investigate the change while the context is still fresh.

API contracts become harder to maintain when several teams contribute to the same system.

For example, a company might have separate teams responsible for:

If nobody owns an API contract, small changes can create unexpected problems for other teams.

Assigning clear ownership helps establish who reviews changes, maintains documentation, and coordinates breaking updates.

This becomes particularly important when an organization expands its engineering capacity across locations or adds several specialized teams. Companies planning that kind of growth may also need to consider enterprise IT recruitment as part of their wider engineering workforce strategy.

Regardless of how a team is assembled, its development process should establish clear responsibilities for API design, versioning, testing, and release coordination.

A few practical conventions can make a significant difference:

Assign an owner to every important API or service.

Document breaking changes before implementation.

Require contract-related tests in pull requests.

Keep generated clients synchronized with the API specification.

Communicate deprecations before removing existing fields.

Monitor production errors after deploying API changes.

These practices help prevent a growing engineering organization from becoming a collection of disconnected services.

API contract drift is not simply a TypeScript problem. It is a coordination problem that becomes visible when applications and services develop different expectations about the same data.

TypeScript provides useful compile-time checks, but it cannot guarantee that an HTTP response matches a declared interface.

A more reliable approach combines several techniques:

Use OpenAPI to document API expectations.

Generate TypeScript clients with tools such as Orval.

Use MSW to test frontend behavior without a live backend.

Use Pact when consumer-provider contract verification is appropriate.

Run validation and tests automatically in CI/CD.

You do not need to introduce every tool at once. Start by validating external API responses, document important endpoints, and gradually automate contract checks as the application grows.

The result is a codebase where developers can make changes with greater confidence and where frontend and backend teams have a shared understanding of how their systems communicate.

#10324. Nintendo Switch 2-ready smart glasses from Viture are at their lowest price ever (up to $160 off)

Viture’s smart display glasses offer official Switch 2 compatibility with the Mobile Dock Mini, and these Black Friday deals even come with free bonus controllers and other accessories.

One of the most annoying things about playing Ocarina of Time right now is that everyone in my home is at a different point in their save file. This makes it tough to be in the same room with others and not spoil something for them, but plugging in a pair of Viture glasses makes this much easier since no one else can see the screen inside the glasses I’m wearing.

You can get your own pair of Viture glasses with the Switch 2 Mobile Dock Mini for as low as $375. This pack comes with Viture Pro 2 glasses, which sport a pair of 120Hz micro-OLED displays with 1,600-nit peak brightness and built-in myopia adjustment diopters. They also weigh just 63g, making them comfortable for long gaming sessions.

The Mobile Dock Mini (on sale for $99 on its own) in the pack comes with a magnetic mount that attaches to the back of the Switch 2. This Dock lets you plug your Viture glasses in and also charges the Switch 2, thanks to the built-in 10,000mAh battery. That delivers more than double the Switch 2’s battery life, so you can clear several temples in Ocarina before even thinking of stopping to charge.

Most of Viture’s glasses are on sale and have extra free gifts, which you can see in the image above. This includes the company’s high-end Viture Beast model, which is on sale for $489 ($60 off). That’s the lowest price ever for the glasses.

Viture Beast upgrades the experience with a wider field of view (58 degrees), native 3DoF spatial tracking, and 9-level electrochromic lens dimming. Native spatial tracking means that you can pin the virtual monitor in space and move around as if it were a TV mounted on a wall. Beast doesn’t have diopters, so you’ll need to order prescription lenses if you need myopia adjustment.

The biggest discount of all is on Viture Luma Pro, which is down to $339 ($160 off). Luma Pro is Viture’s “Goldilocks” pair with excellent image quality and RGB lighting along the frames for some extra style, and even includes myopia adjustment diopters. Pair any of these Viture glasses with the Mobile Dock Mini for Switch 2 compatibility, making them the only pair of smart glasses with official Switch 2 support.

Lastly is Viture Luma Ultra, down to $449 ($150 off). Luma Ultra sports the best image quality of all Viture glasses and includes myopia-adjusting diopters. These are the only pair that support 6DoF tracking when using the Viture Spacewalker app thanks to the cameras on the front, but there’s no native 3DoF support like Beast has, so this functionality is limited to content you view through the app.

Nipponese has semiconductor manufacturing on wheels is an interesting contrast to the U.S.' deployable Burger King trucks.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Multiple nations worldwide have chip-making programs in their respective universities, a discipline that is seeing increasing demand by the day. Japan is one such nation, and it currently has a program in which students can design circuits to wire chip wafers with miniaturized lithography stations. That gear is now going on wheels to schools and companies thanks to mobileFab trucks.

Each truck-mounted mobileFab container contains three machines: a photoresist coater, a maskless lithography machine, and a photoresist developer. Students take pre-etched wafers made by Japan's NIAIST (Institute for Advanced Industrial Science and Technology) and go through the necessary steps to wire the transistors therein together and produce a finalized chip core. The procedures are analogous to getting a breadboard with some pre-mounted, unconnected components and turning that into a product.

The three machines going into trucks are part of the larger Minimal Fab laboratories in place in some Japanese colleges. They're going on the move so that other schools and companies can train students/employees in the art of chipmaking. For now, the 12.5-mm wafers come from the NIAIST, but they can come from other foundries. Each machine is roughly 30 cm wide, and the machines use localized cleaning and sealed between-machine transportation so as not to have to rely on large-scale cleanrooms.

According to the press release by the Minimal Fab Promotion Organization, this system is not only meant for democratizing access to chip manufacturing education. The machines also allow for rapid prototyping and iteration of chip designs, and facilitate small-scale manufacturing — all with modest capital investment.

The "why" of this initiative is fairly predictable: the program's organizers predict that semiconductor fab engineers will be in high demand over the next 10 years, and there aren't even enough teachers going around, making systematic education difficult. Additionally, the division of labor in semiconductor fabs means that many engineers don't participate in all stages of the chip-making process, nor do they have opportunities to operate chip-making equipment themselves. The mobileFab will be on display at the SEMICON Japan 2026 conference in December.

#10319. Shared CXL memory pools come with steep software tax that could stall multi-server scaling

The results land as memory makers push shared CXL pools as a home for AI’s KV cache.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Researchers at the University of Texas at Arlington and Intel measured what happens when four servers share one pool of CXL memory on real hardware. In a presentation shared at Supercomputer 2026 (SC26), they found that because the hardware doesn’t automatically keep shared data updated across servers, necessary software overhead adds a 3-5µ (microsecond) delay per lock, each time servers access the same data. These minute delays effectively cancel out the benefits — a finding that comes as CXL memory pools are being proposed as a potential AI KV cache solution.

Locks work like traffic signals for shared data: a server has to claim the lock before it changes something in the pool, and the other servers wait until it releases it. This way, no two servers overwrite the same data at the same time. Within a given server, the CPU’s hardware handles that handoff in a fraction of a microsecond, but across these servers, software is in charge of enforcement.

The setup comprises four 86-core Intel Xeon 6787P servers with 256GB of DRAM each, connected over PCIe 5.0 to one CXL memory box. The switch, which UT Arlington’s Peiran Du called “the only commercially available product we can use,” caps their setup at four servers. The catch is that there is no cross-host cache coherence or atomic operations on “a real four-host CXL shared-memory system.”

This means no synced CPU caches and no hardware atomics between servers to build locks on, so software has to handle both. Writers publish their cached copy out to the pool and wait for it to finish, while readers throw out stale copies before reading, with the locks built from plain reads and writes, such as Lamport’s fast mutex. CXL 3.0 defines a hardware fix for the caches, called Back-Invalidate, but the researchers hadn’t received vendor confirmation that their platform supports it.

Aside from the lock acquisition penalty, which is “roughly an order of magnitude higher than local hardware spin locks,” there is a visibility cost: “one-way cross-host visibility is about 1 µs.” This is 0.94 µs, one way, compared to 1.91 µs for an RDMA write on their 400Gb/s InfiniBand, so the link isn’t the cause. A local compare-and-swap takes about 100 ns and, across servers, a lock’s median is 3.7 µs if uncontended, but 132 µs at the 95th percentile with several servers on one lock.

The result: breadth-first search (BFS), a standard graph algorithm and a common benchmark, “gains nothing from adding a second host,” and was actually slower on four servers than on one, at 0.74s versus 0.55s. This was mostly not from the locks and barriers, which were only about 3.5% of its runtime, but due to the repeated flushing of shared state at every level.

On the other hand, throughput for a hash table — using independent buckets and per-host allocators — grew almost linearly when adding hosts. Triangle counting, another standard graph benchmark, also had a runtime reduction of more than half when scaling from one to four hosts.

Those costs matter, in part, because shared CXL pools are emerging as a new home for KV cache — an AI model’s stored record of a conversation’s state — once it outgrows GPU memory and a server’s own DRAM. The CXL Consortium’s SC26 session description says cloud providers and GPU makers “have highlighted CXL memory pooling as an effective approach for improving KV cache access.”

SK hynix, which makes CXL memory modules, showed a design that hands KV cache between GPU servers through a shared pool and claims 2.6x faster time to first token than standard RDMA setups. Its abstract also claims 3.0x lower P99 latency and 1.9x higher throughput. Micron, at SC26’s CXL Pavilion, showed its Abaco reference design of pooled CXL memory shared across rack servers and GPUs. It claimed 10x to 30x agentic AI gains, with famfs support for apps like Nvidia’s Dynamo.

The need is real, even if efficiency gains have led to less cache needed per token. Vikram Sharma Mailthody of Nvidia Research said at SC26’s Emerging Storage panel that his own analysis of open models on Hugging Face shows KV per token falling “by 50% every twelve months” with “up to 78 times reduction so far,” giving the example that 128K context took “about 64 gigabytes” three years ago and now takes less than one. But context lengths are heading toward millions of tokens, and “the product of those two will keep increasing,” he said.

Agents also add to the demand. Earlier in the conference, a workshop talk by Argonne National Laboratory and RIT researchers, based on public AI serving traces, showed that a “session calls again ~2 min later, once its tools return: a 160 GiB recency cache keeps 1% of its context,” needing the GPU to recompute the rest, or about 99%. Recomputation is significantly slower and more demanding, and memory is needed to cache more.

That makes it a capacity problem more than a speed problem. “Memory capacity is becoming a dominant factor. Memory latencies have not been seen as a primary problem yet,” Mailthody said. An agent’s context only has to survive a gap of a couple of minutes. It’s also ideal for any KV cache solution to be as inexpensive as possible, and given that a 128GB DIMM costs more than four times that of a 64GB DIMM last year. According to Intel’s Anil Godbole on SC26’s CXL panel, being able to add capacity past the DIMM slot limit — including reusing DDR4 — bolsters the case for CXL even further.

It doesn’t hurt that the KV cache handoff is write-once, read-many, which is the type of pattern that actually scaled in testing, although UT Arlington did not specifically test KV cache. Researchers behind OCEAN, a CXL emulator, backed this idea in the same paper session as UT Arlington, saying that software coherence is fine for read-heavy work, with hardware essential as writes climb. Its abstract reports that hardware coherence, at least in emulation, can give an 11x improvement at full coverage on Tigon database workloads.

Limitations still exist, which is why SK hynix, for one, is relying on “novel locking and coherence protocols” for its design. Hardware isn’t quite there yet, and Back-Invalidate might “be pretty costly,” Du said, suggesting that both hardware and software coherence may be required.

Micron, which built prototype KV cache sharing into Nvidia’s Dynamo, noted two primary failure cases in a CXL Consortium presentation last month: where the writer’s data never reaches the pool, and where the reader never sees the updates. The first can be fixed by producers flushing before blocks are published, so unflushed blocks can never be found. The second is fixed with a consumer flush, that is, invalidation of their cached lines, before reading. These are the fixes and costs that UT Arlington was measuring.

Micron cut its flushing cost by flushing each slot only once, which works because KV cache is content-addressed — a slot in the pool that hasn’t changed stays coherent after its first flush. Micron’s presentation also notes that neither failure causes a crash. Instead, the read returns plausible-looking data, and the output is wrong in subtle ways, with the wrong tokens on some requests under cache pressure.

Working against CXL as a solution is the fact that the memory pooling only reaches within a rack today, Godbole said; it doesn’t span a full data center. Marvell and Penguin Solutions, in collaboration and in addition to others like Lightelligence, have shown or announced memory expansion and pooling over optical links, which could stretch pooling past a single rack. CXL is also “not the protocol to ferry such big data,” Godbole added, as it’s built for smaller reads and writes, 64 bytes at a time, closer to how a CPU uses RAM. For bulk transfers, he said, RDMA is more efficient.

A research system called Beluga, in a paper published on arXiv a year ago, had KV cache in “a commercial CXL switch-based memory pool” with time to first token cut by 89.6% and throughput raised 7.35x compared with an RDMA-based setup once its cache was filled. This suggests some optimization could improve the usefulness of the technology, too.

CXL is clearly a hit or miss with how it is actually used being a main concern, with “a gap between the [CXL] spec and the implementation from different vendors,” according to UT Arlington’s Jia Rao. SK hynix’s second-generation CMM-DDR5, at 256GB and using CXL 3.2, has only been shown, and the device its KV cache design uses to select what to send is still what the company’s Younghoon Min called a “research prototype.” These are early times, and the enterprise landscape is simultaneously changing quickly.

On paper, shared CXL pools do fit the KV handoff idea, but until a commercial switch ships with confirmed coherence across servers, the best we have is KV cache numbers from vendor demos and research prototypes. Back-Invalidate should cut the software overhead UT Arlington measured, but Du expects it to add delays of its own; production systems would likely need a combination of hardware coherence and software approaches like Micron’s.

#10316. 10 Best AI App Builders I've Used in 2026 (and What Each One Gets Wrong)

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

AI App Builders are exploding in popularity, and for good reason. It’s never been easier to build real, functional apps and internal tools using app builders. To test them all, I built the same app on 10 of the most popular AI app builders and tested each across usability, cost, correctness, and ease of use. Most of them can turn a paragraph of description into something that looks like software within a single session. The differences show up around the tenth prompt, when you learn what each edit costs and who has to fix the code once something breaks. I took every price from the vendor's own pricing page on October 29, 2026.

TLDR: Of the best AI app builders I've used, Softr is the one I'd hand to a team that needs auth, data, user groups or integrations. The other nine I tested include code generators such as Lovable and Bolt and visual platforms such as Bubble and Glide, and each one carries a cost or upkeep trade-off worth seeing before you commit.

I looked at the same seven things in every tool, from the first prompt onward:

Softr gets used a lot by operations and business teams as their AI app builder for secure client portals, internal tools and other business apps, none of which require code. Write a short brief in your own words, and the AI Co-Builder turns it into a database plus the core app that sits on it: tables, pages and layouts, the data connections behind them, plus user groups and permissions, so real users can sign in from day one. Workflows come as the next step, either by prompting the Co-Builder again or by adding them in the visual editor.

The Free plan is $0 for unlimited apps, with room for 5 app users, 3 builders, 5,000 records and 5 AI credits each month. Basic runs $19 per month, Pro $99 and Business $329, all on annual billing. Enterprise pricing is custom and includes SSO and SCIM for organizations managing access at scale. The full plan table sits on Softr's pricing page.

Lovable builds full-stack web apps through conversation, writing React code while it takes care of hosting, SSL and the backend. It's designed to move a founder or product team from a prompt to a shareable prototype, and the preview updates as the agent works.

Base44 calls itself a no-code AI platform: you explain the app, and it generates the structure, design and logic while running the backend itself. Authentication, a database and analytics come on every plan, Free included.

Base44 is free for 25 message credits a month. Starter costs $16 per month and Builder $40 per month, both on annual billing, with Pro at $80 and Elite at $160.

Bolt is a coding agent that writes full-stack projects in the browser and runs them on Bolt Cloud, which supplies hosting, databases and integrations. It suits people who want to watch the code take shape and edit it themselves.

Bolt Free is $0 with 1M tokens a month and Bolt branding. Pro costs $25 per month with 10M tokens, and Teams runs $30 a month for each member on monthly billing.

Replit pairs its Agent with a cloud workspace, so a description turns into a running app whose sign-in, database, hosting and monitoring come wired up. The homepage pitches it to people who don't code, though the result underneath is a code project.

Core costs $20 per month ($18 with annual billing) and Pro costs $100 per month ($90 with annual billing). Enterprise is custom and adds SSO, SCIM and audit logs.

Glide starts internal business apps from whatever you hand it, whether a spreadsheet, a written prompt or a PDF, and its newer platform, GlideOS, reads a sheet's structure and relationships to draft screens and workflows. Its apps grew up on phones, and that heritage still shapes the product.

Glide Free is $0 with limited credits. Basic costs $25 per month, Plus $50 per month and Pro $125 per month; annual billing isn't offered yet, according to Glide.

Bubble Free gives you 50K workload units and 500 AI credits each month. Web plans run $32 per month for Starter, $119 for Growth and $349 for Team, all on annual billing.

Retool is an internal tools engine aimed at engineering teams. You describe or assemble an app that connects straight to production databases, APIs and LLMs, with auth and access controls in place at deployment.

v0 generates full-stack Next.js web apps from a prompt and deploys them to Vercel, with Design Mode for visual tweaks and GitHub sync for the code. It's designed around a developer's workflow.

v0's Free plan gives new users $5 of one-time credits and caps messages at 7 per day. Plus runs $30 a month per user, and Business $100 a month per user.

Figma Make turns prompts and Figma design context into code-backed prototypes and web apps you can publish at a URL. It can also scaffold a Payload backend with a database, APIs, auth and an admin panel, or connect to Supabase for sign-in and stored data.

Figma's Starter plan is free with up to 500 AI credits a month. Figma lists a Professional Full seat at $16 per month with 3,000 AI credits, and Organization Full seats cost $55 per month on annual billing.

Collins Dictionary named "vibe coding" its Word of the Year for 2025, and the phrase now covers any workflow where you describe software in plain language and an AI produces it. AI app builders package that workflow with hosting, data and sign-in, so a non-developer can get from idea to something clickable without installing anything.

The questions buyers ask have turned plainer since then: what each edit costs, who keeps the app running, and whether a client can sign in and see their own records alone. A generated front end makes a good demo, and a team using it every day needs permissions and a predictable bill for the next hundred edits.

Softr is now my default when recommending AI app builders. It handles teams, auth, and real company data better than any other product. The AI Co-Builder drafts tables, pages and user groups, workflows follow as the next step, and the app keeps running on maintained platform components with no codebase to patch. App-user pricing and an editor that works without AI credits keep later changes from turning into a running meter.

Three situations call for a different tool. Glide makes a better mobile-first choice when the app spends its days on phones in the field. Bubble gives more front-end design freedom when a project calls for bespoke layouts, interactive animation or heavy brand styling. If your engineers want version control and audit logs and can handle a technical setup, Retool covers that need.

Agents are moving inside the apps these tools produce. Gartner expects task-specific AI agents inside 40% of enterprise applications by the close of 2026, against under 5% in 2025, so a 2027 app builder will need to host agents that respect the same permissions as human users.

Building is also leaving the builder's own window. The Model Context Protocol now sits under the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation and reports more than 97 million SDK downloads a month, with client support in ChatGPT and Claude, among others. Softr's changelog dates its official Claude and ChatGPT connector to October 6, 2026, and I expect more teams to start an app from the chat assistant they already use.

The caution comes from Gartner too: it predicts organizations will scrap upward of 40% of agentic AI projects before 2028, citing escalating costs, unclear business value and inadequate risk controls. Going into 2027, I'd judge any builder on whether it keeps agent costs and access rules visible to the team running the app.

Neville Naidoo is a technology journalist covering AI, startups, and the digital economy, with a focus on how emerging technologies are constantly evolving and shaping our everyday life.

#10315. Samsung might copy the iPhone’s Dynamic Island soon, but it actually looks good [Video]

A new leak suggests that Samsung is preparing to copy the iPhone’s Dynamic Island feature in the not-too-distant future, to an extent that not many other Android brands have even done thus far.

Copying the Dynamic Island was briefly like a rite of passage for some Android brands, with many wasting almost no time in delivering their own version of the feature. But, on many of those devices, it’s a surface-level ripoff at best. The feature is primarily limited to music apps and timers, rarely working with any third-party apps in meaningful ways. Android has a built-in feature similar to Apple’s but not in the same styling.

Samsung is now preparing its own version of the Dynamic Island, and it seems this one has a bit more meat on its bones.

SamMobile on Twitter/X posted a video and two still images of what appears to be a Dynamic Island clone coming to Galaxy devices. It’s mentioned as potentially coming to the Galaxy S27 series (so, One UI 9.5) and being called “Moment Effects.” A portion of the software explicitly mentions integration with Google Sports, the leak claims, while it seems Samsung is using Live Notifications here, which already support a number of third-party apps.

The current implementation of live activities showing the "chip" in the top bar is honestly far from good.

It negates one of the major pros of Android over iOS: being able to see notification icons in the top bar.

As when the "chip" of the live activity is active/shown, all notification icons will get hidden, even if there's a ton of space left between the "chip" and the constraint of the front camera area - an implementation that makes no sense whatsoever.

I honestly can't fathom how could Google come out with such poor implementation.

I don't particularly like this one from Samsung, but it surely is 1000000 times better from a UX perspective.

The kicker from a UX perspective is that Samsung’s interpretation allows you to swipe between activities, similar to Apple, but the core premise is similar with the island showing around the selfie camera cutout.

When this feature might surface does remain unclear, but a One UI 9.5 debut would make plenty of sense. That update is in beta now and due to launch on the Galaxy S27 series early next year.

What do you think of Samsung’s alleged Dynamic Island clone? Personally, I’m on board as long as it proves useful, and it seems to be on the right track compared to most other copycats.

#10313. Galaxy Z Fold 8 features: What you can do on a foldable

Folding phones have come in numerous variations over the years as the concept has evolved. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is the latest evolution that introduces a form factor that fits every user. Its unique design makes it a foldable most people can actually use – which makes it a perfect gift. You might be surprised by what it can do.

It’s in the name. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 folds and unfolds like other foldable devices – that much you know. But what the Galaxy Z Fold 8’s form factor provides is something different to what most might be familiar with.

Instead of a tall device that unfolds into a near-uniform square display, you get a wider screen more like a tablet. That makes it perfect for watching videos or movies. Content that naturally works well on TVs or your computer will look great on the Galaxy Z Fold 8.

What about content that’s best viewed in portrait mode? Because it opens up to a tablet-like display, you can turn the Fold 8 to watch YouTube Shorts or Instagram Reels without a problem, so if you or someone you know likes to watch content on a bigger display, the Z Fold 8 makes that much easier. It really doesn’t matter what content you come across – the wider inner display gives you that large screen feeling.

Like a well-designed tool, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 has more purposes than the tasks best suited for the inner display. That shorter, wider profile makes the outer display smaller, but not as thin as something on other foldables, like the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra.

In reality, the aspect ratio is similar enough across both the inner and outer screens that most content scales well on the shorter front panel. Social apps like X and Instagram look great because videos and images are able to fill the screen, rather than squeeze. Samsung’s One UI software also supports app optimization across both screens, although the experience may vary by app.

Saying the Galaxy Z Fold 8’s outer display is “minimal” isn’t a dig, either. Apps can be refreshing to use when you don’t need to open them on a large scale. Take Messages, for instance. It’s not a complex app, and there isn’t a ton to see – just the last couple of messages exchanged. The same goes for plenty of apps available on the Google Play Store.

And guess what? If you don’t like using the app on a smaller display, just unfold the phone. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is such a versatile phone, whether it’s a gift during the holidays or one for yourself.

There are instances where you need the large real estate. One UI 9 gives the Galaxy Z Fold 8 the option to open and run multiple apps on your screen. There are several ways you can do it, too.

The main approach is to split two apps on the wide inner display. But if you want to see more from one app, you can simply drag the split over in one direction. One UI 9 leaves room to add one more app to that split screen, giving you a three-way Split View. All it takes is dragging an app from the taskbar and choosing the spot.

If you truly need a fourth app open, you have the option to open another in a floating window. Having four apps open at once is definitely a niche instance, but the Galaxy Z Fold 8 handles it like it’s nothing. You can have YouTube up in one corner while you check Messages for gift ideas and shop through the Amazon app. It might be helpful to keep a list of what you got and for whom in a floating Sheets window.

The point is not only that it’s technically possible, but it’s usable. So often devices let users open apps in split screen, but are in no way comfortable enough for the task. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is perfect for it, and the experience actually makes you more productive, not less.

Most phones don’t let you get the best angle without any sort of third-party accessory. The Galaxy Z Fold 8, though, acts like its own tripod in a way.

Let’s say you’re taking photos, and you need to get a shot of yourself, but no one is around to take the photo for you. The Galaxy Z Fold 8’s hinge lets it prop itself up, so you can do things like set a timer and run to strike a pose.

This comes in handy for videos, too. Think of how many times you wanted to get a good angle on a plane or somewhere where there’s this flat surface just asking for a tiny tripod or kickstand. Well, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is its own kickstand and can be positioned at just the right angle.

You can get the Galaxy Z Fold 8 from your favorite carriers and retailers, but Best Buy is one of the leading places to find deals during the holiday season. You’ll find hefty discounts, higher trade-in values for your old devices, and more.
