Thankfully, there were no reported incidents of this vulnerability causing damage or injury before it was patched.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

After noticing that his Elecbrakes remote had automatically paired to a stranger's trailer, Patrick Forck's cybersecurity spider senses tingled. Any feelings of foreboding were warranted, as it was discovered that a critical Bluetooth security flaw meant anyone could connect to an Elecbrakes controller "without pairing, authentication, a PIN, or any approval." Over the following 10 months, Forck and his Element Digital colleague Jeremy McCarthy would fully identify the vulnerabilities, make responsible disclosures to the vendor, work on fix verification, and more.

The story goes that Forck was a contented user of the Elecbrakes solution for the trailer towing fraternity. The firm's systems are claimed to be easy DIY plug-and-play controllers for enhanced braking response – important for trailer towing, especially with larger and heavier loads. The core functionality wasn't a problem, but Forck was alarmed when driving down the highway one day and noticed that his Elecbrakes In-Car Remote had connected to someone else’s trailer. "It had connected mid-drive, without pairing or a prompt, to a brake controller that wasn’t mine, on a trailer I’d never seen, belonging to a driver who had no idea," explained our tech-savvy protagonist. It wasn't long before he thought, "If a device I don’t own will happily talk to my in-car remote driving past with zero friction… what exactly is stopping my phone or any other Bluetooth device from talking back?" Clearly, Elecbrakes ' ease of use was unintentionally too powerful.

Forck and McCarthy's first step on the road to a solution was to use Claude to do the heavy lifting on the reverse engineering of the Elecbrakes Android app. McCarthy built a Web Bluetooth research tool that runs in Chrome, again using Claude. Then Forck tested the newly built tool with his car and trailer on some gravel roads on his family estate. It was confirmed that any attacker could connect via Bluetooth from nearby without Bluetooth pairing or authentication. Moreover, they could send simple commands to the trailer, apply braking at any force level, and receive confirmation that the brake had engaged.

As per the blog post documenting the finding and fixing of these vulnerabilities, the danger of a security flaw which "outputs torque to a wheel on a public road," is difficult to overstate. Especially when the attack surface and opportunity are open to “anyone within Bluetooth range.”

With the bulk of research complete, the Element Digital colleagues disclosed the information to Elecbrakes in May 2026. They were pleased with the small firm's responsiveness and openness. By July, firmware updates to patch the EB2 and VM1 models currently on the market were released.

An older Elecbrakes controller called the ELBC 2000 was discovered to have the same Bluetooth security flaws. The vulnerability of this model, which hasn't been sold for a number of years, has now been confirmed by the maker. Nevertheless, some folks will be using it on public roads. Elecbrakes has advised owners to keep an eye on firmware update notices for an impending fix.

The Odyssey G60H monitor breaks the 1 KHz barrier when flipped to HD mode.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Samsung's display business has produced some incredible screens, often with groundbreaking features. We have one such example released today: the Samsung Odyssey G60H (LS27HG602ENXZA), a 27" Fast IPS LCD gaming monitor whose standout feature is that it can refresh up to 1,100 times per second. That is 0.91 milliseconds per frame. This exotic screen isn't cheap, but if you're expecting a price to match the max refresh, be surprised, as you can snag it on Amazon for $894.

If you look at the specifications, you'll see Samsung describe it as a 600Hz gaming monitor. There's no overclocking shenanigans here; this is a "Dual Mode" monitor, meaning that in its native QHD resolution (2560×1440), it supports an already scorching 600Hz refresh rate. You have to slash the resolution by 75% to get that 1100Hz figure, down to just 1280×720, or "HD". Given that this is exactly 1/4 the resolution of QHD, Samsung has hopefully implemented some pretty fancy integer upscaling.

Aside from the resolution and refresh rate specs, this is actually a fairly standard IPS LCD gaming monitor. That's not a knock; it's perfectly fine, with a typical brightness of 400 cd/m², claimed 99% sRGB coverage, rated 1000:1 native contrast, and some measure of HDR10 support—although given the lack of local dimming and the modest brightness, it's hard to call this an HDR display. Naturally, it supports FreeSync Premium and is G-Sync Compatible, and while Samsung doesn't share the VRR ranges, it does say that you can't hit the peak 1,100 refresh rate with FreeSync enabled.

The firm does say that the G60H is the first to include "Odyssey Clear Motion," a feature that it says "reduces motion blur to help players see fast-moving action more clearly during critical moments in gameplay." It's not completely clear what this feature actually is, but Samsung says that "through the optimised blur reduction algorithm, the Odyssey G6 keeps fast-changing scenes clear and crisp."

Samsung notes that it plans to bring the technology to more gaming monitor models, which sounds interesting. Black frame insertion (BFI) and backlight strobing are the two most common methods of motion blur reduction, but Samsung has sold monitors with strobing for over ten years; it would be odd to reintroduce it as a new feature now.

There's an interesting question hanging over this feature: at 1,100Hz, does a monitor even need dedicated motion blur reduction? Blur Busters has long discussed 1,000Hz as something of a milestone for sample-and-hold displays, arguing that sufficiently high refresh rates can approach the motion clarity of a CRT without requiring backlight strobing.

1,000Hz isn't some magical threshold where motion blur disappears entirely, though. That site's own calculations still predict about one pixel of motion blur for every 1,000 pixels per second of movement at 1ms persistence, and that's assuming instantaneous pixel transitions (like an OLED). At 1,100Hz, that drops to about 0.91 pixels, which is certainly impressive, but not quite zero. The monitor's actual pixel response times also factor into the equation, of course, and Samsung's claimed 1ms GtG response time is actually a measured range of 1.00 to 1.99ms, rounded down to a whole number. I'd be shocked if the real pixel response times weren't more like 3-5ms in the worst case.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Whatever the case with the motion blur feature, in terms of connectivity, the Odyssey G6 can accept video through DisplayPort 2.1 or HDMI 2.1. It has two full-sized HDMI ports, and it also has a USB Type-B connector to pass through its pair of USB Type-A ports to the host machine. Curiously, no USB Type-C connectivity is to be found anywhere, which is unusual on a monitor of this price class, but given that this is clearly aimed at desktop gamers who have the hardware to push games to these kinds of frame rates (at least, with frame generation), it's a sensible omission to be sure, as is the elision of integrated speakers. There is a headphone jack to pass-through HDMI audio, though.

The other important characteristics you might like to know are that the Odyssey G6 (G60)'s included stand supports tilt, swivel, pivot, and height adjustments; it supports 100×100 VESA mounting, and that it uses an external AC adaptor, not an internal power supply, which is bad for convenience but good for repairability.

While the image quality is not going to blow you away if you're accustomed to OLEDs, having seen a 540-Hz display in person and been gobsmacked by it, 1,100 Hz sounds absolutely tantalizing. Admittedly, 1280x720 is a low resolution, but we used to play 240p console games on titanic projection TVs. Hardcore competitive gamers don't need high resolutions, so every cut to input lag helps.

#10305. Top 6 AI Detector Tools in 2026: Features, Accuracy Claims and When to Trust Them

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

AI writing tools are now part of everyday work for students, marketers, developers and editors, and a parallel category of tools has appeared to answer one question: was this text written by a person or a model? Teachers, publishers, hiring teams and content managers use these detectors to screen submissions, but the technology is probabilistic, its accuracy claims vary, and the cost of a wrong call can be high.

This guide compares six AI detector tools, CudekAI, GPTZero, Copyleaks, Originality.ai, Turnitin and Sapling, on what their own pages state. It then explains how detectors work, summarizes the research on their limits, and ends with a short script you can use to test any detector on your own samples. The tools are listed in no ranking order. Feature details, limits and prices change often, so confirm current information on each vendor’s site before you commit.

• A detector gives a probability, not proof. Every vendor in this list warns that results can be wrong, and several advise against using a score alone.

• Limits differ widely. Character limits, supported languages, models detected and free allowances vary between tools and even between pages of the same tool.

• Bias and short text are known weak spots. Research has found detectors misclassify some non-native English writing, and most vendors say accuracy improves with longer text.

• Vendor accuracy claims are not comparable. Figures come from different datasets, thresholds and models, so test on your own material.

• Use detection as one signal. Combine it with drafts, version history, interviews or other evidence before acting on a result.

CudekAI’s AI detector returns an AI percentage and a human percentage for pasted text, with paragraph, sentence and word-level analysis for mixed documents. According to its page, it also accepts PDF and Word files with per-page scores and downloadable reports, and offers separate code and image detectors. The page lists models it says it detects, including ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Llama, DeepSeek and Grok, and says it supports more than 100 languages.

Strengths: sentence-level highlighting, file uploads with reports, and extra detectors for code and images in the same product.

Limitations and gaps: the page shows different character limits in different places, including 1,000, 5,000 and 15,000, so check the limit that applies to your plan. It says to start free but does not state a free allowance, and it lists detection as costing one credit. A headline accuracy figure of 99 percent appears in its page metadata, while the body refers to independent benchmarking without naming sources, and its FAQ says accuracy may vary for mixed or paraphrased text and that false positives can occur. API access is listed under an enterprise plan.

Fits: writers and teams who want a quick check with sentence-level detail and file reports, and who will verify results rather than rely on a single percentage.

GPTZero gives an overall score and highlights flagged sentences, and adds a Writing Replay feature that records the writing process, including typing patterns and paste events. It also lists a plagiarism checker and integrations with Google Docs, Google Classroom, Canvas, Zapier and a Chrome extension, plus an API.

Strengths: process-based evidence through Writing Replay, strong education integrations and published benchmark figures. On the RAID benchmark, the page reports 95.7 percent of AI text detected and 1 percent of human text wrongly flagged.

Limitations and gaps: it claims full support for five languages (English, German, Portuguese, French and Spanish) and says other languages lack stated accuracy levels. The company’s own page says no detector is 100 percent accurate, that results should not be the final verdict, and that accuracy is higher on longer English text. The free scan box has a 10,000-character limit, and plan prices are not listed on the page.

Fits: educators and editors who want writing-process evidence as well as a score.

Copyleaks describes an AI detector covering more than 30 languages and models including ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek and Llama. Its AI Logic feature explains why text was flagged, and it says it can detect AI-generated code. It offers a browser extension, a Google Docs add-on, learning-management-system integrations and an enterprise API.

Strengths: explanation of flagged text, code detection, broad integrations and published per-language accuracy figures, which range from 93.08 percent for Portuguese to 99.20 percent for English on AI text, according to the page.

Limitations and gaps: the figures are the vendor’s own. It claims a 0.03 percent false-positive rate and cites a 2023 study, so treat the number as a claim to verify on your data. Free scans cover up to 25,000 characters, but paid plan prices sit on a separate pricing page.

Fits: organizations that need multilingual coverage, code detection or integrations.

Originality.ai combines AI detection with a plagiarism checker and a fact and hallucination checker. It lists sentence-level highlights, a mixed AI and human category in its newer detection models, a Chrome extension with a writing replay feature and an AI detection API.

Strengths: several checks in one product, an API with documentation and a clear statement of limits. The page acknowledges false positives, says very short text under a 100-word minimum and AI rewriting tools can affect results, and advises against using the score alone.

Limitations and gaps: it is credit-based, free scans are capped at 100 credits per account and credits expire two years after purchase. Its accuracy claims cite third-party studies and internal benchmarks that you should review yourself.

Fits: publishers, agencies and SEO teams that want detection, plagiarism and fact checks in one workflow.

Turnitin is built for educators and institutions. Its AI writing detection estimates how much of a submission is human-written versus likely AI-generated, including likely AI-paraphrased content, and works inside learning-management systems alongside similarity checking.

Strengths: deep institutional integration and unusually explicit framing of results as probabilities. For documents above its 300-word minimum, the page reports false-positive rates of 0.014 for English language learners and 0.013 for native English writers and concludes there is no statistically significant bias. It also links guidance on handling suspected false positives.

Limitations and gaps: it is aimed at institutions rather than individual freelancers, the page does not give an overall false-positive figure, and it describes detection as just one piece of a broader challenge. Mention of language support is limited, with a linked post about Arabic.

Fits: schools and universities that already use Turnitin and want detection within the same workflow.

Sapling offers an AI content detector with a free check of the first 2,000 characters, and Pro and Enterprise accounts can check up to 100,000 characters. It provides a free API key and documentation, and it publishes unusually candid guidance on limits.

Strengths: transparent caveats and a developer-friendly API. The page says false positives and negatives may occur, that accuracy varies with dataset, text length and threshold, and advises measuring results on your own examples. It also warns that some tools claiming to be undetectable falsely say they passed its detector.

Limitations and gaps: accuracy improves after about 50 words, non-English text is scored by the English model for unsupported languages and is described as less reliable, and prices are not listed on the page. A reported 60 percent drop in false positives comes from internal evaluations that the page does not publish.

Fits: developers and teams that want to integrate detection and test it on their own data.

The table summarizes what each page states. It is not a benchmark, and “not stated” means the page did not say, not that the feature is absent.

• False positives. Human writing can be flagged, especially when it is short, formulaic or highly predictable.

• Bias risk. A research paper titled GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers found that the detectors it tested consistently misclassified non-native English writing as AI-generated, and warned against using such detectors in educational settings. Turnitin’s page reports the opposite for its own tool, which is a reason to test on your population.

• Evasion. Paraphrasing or editing AI text can lower scores. The same research found that simple prompting strategies could both reduce bias and get text past detectors.

• Mixed authorship. A document that is partly AI-assisted can get a low overall score while individual sentences score high, as Sapling’s page points out.

• Moving targets. New models change the text distribution, so a tool trained on older models can lose accuracy.

• Shifting benchmarks. Vendors report different datasets and thresholds, so numbers are not comparable.

OpenAI’s own experience is a useful reminder. Its AI text classifier correctly flagged 26 percent of AI-written text on a challenge set while mislabeling 9 percent of human text, and the page states that the classifier was withdrawn on July 20, 2023 due to its low rate of accuracy. Detection has improved since, but the underlying difficulty has not gone away.

Most detectors are classifiers trained on large collections of human-written and machine-generated text. They look for statistical patterns, such as how predictable the word choices are or how uniform the sentence structure is, and output a probability. Some systems add features such as sentence-level scoring, writing-process data, or checks for hidden provenance signals.

• Statistical signals. Text that a language model finds highly predictable tends to look machine-like, which is why formulaic human writing can be misflagged.

• Trained classifiers. Detectors learn from labeled examples and update as new models appear.

• Writing-process evidence. Tools such as Writing Replay record how a document was typed or pasted, which is stronger evidence than a style score.

• Provenance. Standards such as C2PA Content Credentials aim to record the origin and edits of content when the creating tool supports them, which is different from guessing after the fact.

Because vendor figures are not comparable, the most reliable approach is to measure. Build a small labeled set that reflects your real content, including human writing from different groups of authors, and calculate false-positive and false-negative rates by group. The script below wraps any detector behind a single function. The stub is a placeholder, so replace it with a call to the tool you are evaluating and follow that vendor’s API documentation.

is_ai: bool        # ground truth you control

group: str = "all" # e.g. "native", "non-native", "technical"

def evaluate(detect, samples, threshold=0.5):

"""detect(text) -> probability the text is AI-generated (0..1).

Wrap any vendor API or tool export in this function."""

g = stats.setdefault(s.group, {"fp": 0, "human": 0, "fn": 0, "ai": 0})

g["fn"] += not flagged          # AI text that slipped through

g["fp"] += flagged              # human text wrongly flagged

fpr = g["fp"] / g["human"] if g["human"] else float("nan")

fnr = g["fn"] / g["ai"] if g["ai"] else float("nan")

print(f"{group:12} false positive rate {fpr:.1%}  false negative rate {fnr:.1%}")

return 0.9 if "delve" in text.lower() else 0.2

Sample("Let us delve into the topic.", True, "native"),

Sample("I wrote this note by hand.", False, "native"),

Sample("We delve into methods used here.", False, "non-native"),

Sample("The results were reviewed twice.", True, "non-native"),

With only a handful of samples the numbers mean little, so use a larger, representative set and report results per group, because an acceptable overall rate can hide a high rate for one group.

• Never treat a score as proof. Use it to start a conversation, not end one.

• Gather corroborating evidence. Drafts, version history, writing-process data and discussion with the author carry more weight than a percentage.

• Tell people how detection is used. Publish a policy so authors know what to expect and how to appeal.

• Check for bias. Test on writers like those you evaluate, including non-native speakers.

A tool that estimates how likely a piece of text is to have been generated by an AI model, usually as a percentage, often with sentence-level highlighting.

They can be useful, but accuracy depends on the text, length, language and threshold, and every vendor in this guide states that errors can occur. Test on your own samples.

Yes. False positives are acknowledged by vendors and documented in research, particularly for short or formulaic text and some non-native English writing.

Free tiers are fine for a quick check, but they have limits on length and features, and the result should not be the sole basis for a decision.

Sometimes. Paraphrasing and editing can lower scores, and partly AI-generated documents can produce mixed results.

A plagiarism checker looks for matches with existing sources. An AI detector estimates whether text resembles machine-generated writing, which is a different and less certain task.

AI detectors are useful screening tools, but none is a verdict. The six reviewed here differ in language coverage, limits, integrations, explainability and how candidly their pages describe error, and their accuracy figures come from different tests. Compare them on the factors that matter for your content, measure false positives on your own samples, and combine any score with other evidence before acting on it.

#10304. Trump’s intervention at Nvidia just gave Democrats another 2028 target

For Democrats eyeing the White House, President Donald Trump’s coziness with tech executives was already a potent target even before he successfully pressured Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang as chief executive.

Now his extraordinary intervention has crystallized their concerns about the growing power of artificial intelligence companies and his blending of government and business interests.

Huang had lost his job because of extramarital affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman suspected of working as a spy for Beijing. Eleven days later, Nvidia’s board put him back in charge.

Although Democrats lack a unified vision for how to handle the proliferation of artificial intelligence, the episode was an opportunity for them to speak largely in unison as they called Huang’s return a threat to national security and described Trump’s role as corrupt.

Nvidia’s decision sends a message “that the national security of this country is not as important as your relationship with President Trump,” said Sen. Ruben Gallego, an Arizona Democrat considering a White House campaign, in an interview with The Associated Press.

“We also have to figure out how corporate America doesn’t take a bad lesson from this, and thinks that somehow it’s OK for them to evade national security for the purposes of just selling more,” Gallego said.

Nvidia is under scrutiny over whether it’s complying with U.S. restrictions on the export of its most advanced semiconductors to China and their use by Chinese tech firms.

The company’s share price dropped sharply during Huang’s brief absence, dragging down the broader stock market to one of its worst weeks since the 2008 financial crisis, before recovering with Monday’s announcement of his reinstatement.

Trump argues that Huang’s leadership at Nvidia is necessary

Still euphoric over their sweeping midterm victories, many ambitious Democrats are still feeling around for the right message on artificial intelligence, which carries both promise and peril as it becomes increasingly intertwined with the economy, infrastructure and daily life.

Trump’s intervention put a spotlight on his own financial stake in the company, which his latest financial disclosure report says was worth at least $12.5 million at the end of 2025, and on the millions of dollars Huang contributed to Trump’s ballroom project.

Writing on social media that “rules should apply to everyone,” California Rep. Ro Khanna noted that “the rich & powerful, like Jensen, do not get to evade export controls or accountability just because it props up the stock price.”

Trump worried that Huang’s ouster was not only tanking the stock market but also risked putting the U.S. behind Beijing in the race for tech dominance.

“I’m doing it for the country,” Trump said on CNBC.

Huang’s reinstatement reinforced the message, which many Democrats delivered in the midterms, that the system is rigged against average Americans, said Sacha Haworth, founder and CEO of The Tech Oversight Project and a former aide to Democrats. Big tech leaders can be a powerful foil.

“They are the most unlikeable men in America, and yet it seems like the system is working very well for them,” Haworth said. “The news this week just reinforced that idea. So the mission that Democrats have now is to continue to prove to voters that they are fighting against this corrupt system, against the influence of tech CEOs and on behalf of Americans.”

Nvidia’s board and Trump himself left no ambiguity over who drove the decision.

It was based on input from “senior levels of the United States government,” Nvidia said in a press release announcing Huang’s return.

Trump said in an interview with CNBC that “I spoke to them, let me just put it that way. And I convinced them.”

Democratic candidates see corruption, security risks

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro tied Huang’s reinstatement to “the sheer corruption and weakness” of the president, calling it “another example of the dangerous combination governing this country: a rigged system that protects those at the very top no matter what, and a corrupt White House that cannot be trusted to put the economic well-being and safety of American families first.”

Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan said that Trump’s pressure campaign made clear that, to the president, “making money is more important than America’s national security or the rule of law.”

Slotkin, a former CIA analyst, added, “If ever there was an issue that deserved national security oversight, it’s this one.”

And Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker drew a comparison between Huang’s reinstatement and Democrats’ broad wins in this month’s midterm elections, calling the CEO’s return an example of “the greed and lack of accountability that the country just rejected.”

Pritzker urged Democrats “to speak with one voice and not be afraid to fight the Trump administration,” saying Trump and Vice President JD Vance “will move mountains for tech billionaires.”

—Jonathan J. Cooper and Meg Kinnard, Associated Press

#10303. The Google Home app is better than Nest alone ever was, mostly

The Nest app is officially dead, but it’s worth taking a step back and remembering that, while there are some rough edges, the Google Home app is a better smart home experience than Nest alone ever could have been.

9to5Google Weekender by Ben Schoon is a part of our free newsletter that also includes ‘Inbox,’ a twice-weekly roundup of key stories from around the web by Daniel Bader. Sign up here to get Weekender delivered to your inbox every Sunday along with ‘Inbox’ on Tuesday and Thursday. You can find past issues here.

The Nest app has been on life support for years now. Google has been migrating legacy products into the Home app for a while and the last few puzzle pieces came in Nest Protect support, the death of the earliest Nest Thermostats, and other assorted adjustments.

Realistically, even long-time Nest users have had no reason to continue using the app over Google Home.

Having been personally, deeply invested in Google’s vision for the smart home over the past decade, I’ll say that the Google Home app we have today is better than the Nest app ever was or ever could be. A huge part of that comes from Google Home’s ability to pull together devices from third-party ecosystems. Being able to control your entire smart home from a single app is how the smart home always should have been, and between Google’s work and the Matter standard, we’re finally able to enjoy that pretty seamlessly for the most part. Automations, Google’s actually-useful AI features, and more only sweeten the deal. I’m also a big fan of what the Home app has become from a UX perspective. While there are always rough edges and bugs to clean up, the customizable homepage and well-organized sections make for a good – not perfect, but good – experience for the end user.

That said, there is one thing that the Nest app’s limited scope benefitted from, and that’s a focus on making your own product great.

Google’s move to the Home app for Nest devices has been a 5-year run of trying to clean things up, improve on the app, and basically bring back the way things were in the Nest app as far as the first-party cameras and thermostats are concerned. It’s taken ages, but we’re finally up to speed, mostly. I still hate that you have to reset Nest Cams to change Wi-Fi when the Nest app just let you change it, and the Nest app’s settings were much less overwhelming, but I’d say the pros far outweigh the cons at this point.

The Nest app was good at its job, but the Google Home app is a worthy successor, finally, and now the Nest app can finally rest. I mostly think the same applies to Gemini vs Google Assistant, with the newer assistant a better overall experience, but it’s easier to poke holes in that argument.

Disagree? What do you think of the Google Home app, and were you still using the Nest app?

The Nvidia board has reinstated Jensen Huang as the company’s CEO just 11 days after he resigned, a move that, although it had strong support from both employees and supporters, had surprised many. While the company’s board of directors voted unanimously to bring the founder back, it seems that this decision was pushed along by pressure from Washington. According to CNN, President Donald Trump, alongside Vice President JD Vance and several members of his cabinet, spent the weekend talking to industry insiders, investors, and even to the board itself to get Jensen back as the chief of Nvidia.

“I’ve been speaking to the board directly and indirectly, and I felt very strongly about it,” Trump said in an interview with CNBC. “I think we have one of our great stars back in play.” Nvidia’s stock price took a beating when Jensen Huang admitted to the affairs, and his future at the company was in question. It went from bad to worse when he finally resigned on November 12, with the rest of the market following. This has brought concerns that Jensen’s downfall would drag Nvidia and the economy with him, which could potentially turn into a catastrophe as the AI bubble pops.

The President said that bringing Jensen back as the CEO of Nvidia would be the only solution to this conundrum. True enough, Nvidia stock prices shot up to around $165 after Jensen’s reinstatement — a more than 25% rally from its previous close of around $130. “It’s a rocket ship going in the right direction, and it’s taking the whole market,” the president added. “It could be that there’s never been anything like it.”

Despite the seemingly positive impact of Jensen Huang’s return to the company, Trump’s decision to intervene in the inner workings of a private institution has raised apprehension among politicians, even those from his own party. The biggest concerns raised include the Nvidia CEO’s involvement in national security issues, including his affair with a suspected Chinese spy, the billions of dollars’ worth of advanced Nvidia chips that have been allegedly smuggled despite the government’s export controls, and the fact that the President assured the Nvidia board that his administration does not believe that Jensen is a threat to national security and that he also was not facing any criminal charges, despite ongoing investigations. People also raised questions about the White House’s influence on the board of directors of a private company, something that was characterized as “an unprecedented campaign.”

Trump’s push for Jensen Huang’s return at Nvidia is inherently risky, with the president himself saying that he had consulted Attorney General Todd Blanche and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton about it. He said that they’ve been studying the issue for quite some time and that they had found nothing wrong, especially as Trump said that he can’t have anyone indicted after making the recommendation.

#10300. BYD’s new car has a disappearing steering wheel—because it can

BYD just killed the steering wheel as we know it. Permanently bolted in front of the driver, it’s a fundamental part of the car. Unless you’re BYD. The Chinese automaker’s new six-seat plug-in hybrid SUV features a disappearing steering wheel that folds itself into a dashboard compartment at the push of a button.

It only needs 10 seconds, then puff, the wheel is gone and the dashboard is clean. The driver suddenly has about 10 more inches of legroom. BYD bills it as the world’s first in a production car. Aside from race cars with their pop-in and pop-out steering wheels, nobody has ever seen anything like this. The magic wheel comes only with the $49,400 Folding Smart Cabin trim of the Tai 9, a model from BYD’s sub-brand Fang Cheng Bao.

During the November 19 launch, Fang Cheng Bao’s general manager, Xiong Tianbo, said that another carmaker floated a folding wheel back in 2016. It wasn’t possible at the time. “It has always been difficult to bring into mass production,” Xiong said. The reason, he explained, is that in a traditional car, “a mechanical steering column connects the steering wheel and the wheels,” adding “that one column limits the imagination for the entire driver’s space.”

The Tai 9 doesn’t need a hard steering column because it uses a steer-by-wire system. Rather than mechanically pushing the road wheels to a new angle through a shaft, a rack, and a pair of tie rods, the system uses a new folding steering wheel that works like a game controller. Turn it, and electronic sensors “read” the movement, sending an electronic signal to the motors that actually turn the road wheels.

The same trim also gets brake-by-wire, which swaps the brakes’ mechanical link for electronic signals, too. This is similar to the fly-by-wire technology that modern fighter airplanes use. Rather than directly driving heavy hydraulic systems, the pilot uses a joystick similar to a computer controller. It sends impulses that get interpreted by a computer, which in turn operates the mechanics of the airplane to make it change direction in the air.

BYD says it has five layers of redundancy covering sensing, control, actuation, communications, and power supply. The Chinese car manufacturer also claims that its folding system has an ASIL D rating (for automotive safety integrity level)—that’s the highest safety level in the risk classification standard for road vehicles as defined by the International Organization for Standardization. BYD sets strict usage conditions and safety interlocks, which means the wheel stays out while the car is being driven and only stows once it’s parked, or while it parks itself.

How it works

Without the metal shaft connecting to the car’s direction, Fang Cheng Bao’s designers had nothing to stop them from playing with the steering wheel in any way they wanted. To pack it inside the dashboard, the steering wheel uses a motorized folding mechanism with a precision hinge that swings through up to 180 degrees.

Once folded, it recedes into the dashboard like Homer Simpson disappearing into a bush. When the wheel emerges, the hinge hides itself. Drivers get a D-shaped rim they can grip all the way around, proper switches, and an adjustable position. Despite the futuristic tech, the wheel should feel familiar.

The muscle behind all this, according to the company, is an automotive-grade brushless motor, the same kind BYD is using in the dexterous hands of its new AI-powered robots. Xiong said the folding cabin took 36 months to develop, and Fang Cheng Bao says its durability tests folded the wheel 96,000 times in various environments, including at room temperature, in the cold, and in the heat.

This thing also folds on its own when you use its self-parking mode—BYD’s autonomous tech that parks your car in any parking garage completely on its own. The wheel retracts on the way into the spot, since nobody is using it, and only returns on the way out of the parking spot to meet its owner. Good boy.

Nap time

With the wheel tucked away, one more button push raises the driver’s seat cushion by about 3.5 inches and tilts the backrest to 165 degrees, all within 20 seconds. The car is now a nap pod. BYD says it put five volunteers in the seat and tracked their sleep for 100 minutes, scoring it by American Academy of Sleep Medicine guidelines. All five drifted into light sleep. Three made it all the way to deep sleep.

According to Xiong, the folding cabin in this trim of the Tai 9—which bundles steer-by-wire, brake-by-wire, the lie-flat driver’s seat, and the folding wheel—is a bet on what comes next: “It’s forward-looking preparation for the era of L3 and L4 intelligent driving.” Level 4 cars may not need a steering wheel, but L3 cars will still need one in case the driver must take control of the car from the car’s AI. 

The Tai 9 isn’t there yet. But it’s siesta-ready. That’s good enough for now.

#10299. Samsung Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 vs Watch 9: When is it right to spend more?

The Samsung Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 is worth spending more on if you want longer battery life, a brighter outdoor display, and specialized features for trail running and diving. The Galaxy Watch 9 is the better fit if you want Samsung’s latest everyday health tools in a smaller, lighter watch.

Both, however, are fantastic smartwatches with limitless potential. They share a Snapdragon Wear Elite processor and many of Samsung’s newest wellness features, so deciding between them is really about figuring out your priorities when it comes to buying a wearable this holiday season. We’re here to help you figure that out.

As we covered in our Galaxy Watch 9 and Watch Ultra 2 comparison, both watches move to Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Wear Elite platform. Both also ship with Wear OS 7 and One UI 8 Watch.

That shared foundation includes useful health insights. Vitals brings overnight measurements together to establish your personal baseline, while Daily Cardio Load helps you understand training demands and recovery. Hearing monitoring can flag potentially unsafe noise levels, whether you’re at a concert or somewhere unexpectedly loud.

Both also get five years of Wear OS updates and security patches, making either a useful long-term partner for your Samsung device, like the Galaxy S26 Ultra or Galaxy Z Fold8.

The clearest differences are size, battery capacity, display brightness, and outdoor capabilities. Here’s how the lineup breaks down:

As you can tell, the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 is considerably bigger and heavier, but you get a lot more capability for that additional size.

The Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 makes its strongest case when your plans regularly take you beyond a desk, a gym, or a charger.

Samsung rates the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 for up to 60 hours with the always-on display enabled, compared with up to 30 hours for the Watch 9, and that extra headroom is appealing when your day starts with a workout and finishes well into the evening.

Then there’s the screen. In our hands-on with both watches, the Ultra 2’s brightness stood out immediately, with a higher peak that gives it an advantage when checking workout information outdoors, even in the bright sun. And its titanium frame provides added durability.

The Ultra 2 also adds Trail Run tracking for elevation and terrain impact, route guidance using compatible GPX files, and Nutrition Alert hydration guidance. These are tangible reasons to upgrade if your usual run involves trails instead of pavement.

Diving is another differentiator. Samsung specifies recreational diving support to depths of up to 40 meters, with automatic tracking of depth, dive time and water temperature — a remarkable feat for a piece of technology that lives on your wrist.

The best choice becomes clearer when you picture your own routine:

Choose the Galaxy Watch 9 for everyday wellness, a lighter fit, and strong value. Choose the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 for longer adventures, more demanding outdoor activities, and greater freedom between charges.

If you’re replacing an older Galaxy Watch, both offer a compelling new generation of health insights and long-term support. Both last a long time and look absolutely awesome with running shorts or a business suit. But the Watch Ultra 2 can take you that extra mile, literally and figuratively, and may be worth spending more on during Best Buy’s Holiday Deals event.

The Bambu Lab P3C is the lower-cost little brother of the H3C. It has the same type of tools and outstanding TPU printing process as its larger sibling, but drops the heated chamber, filament dryer, and automatic filament loading. If you want an upgradable tool changer on a more manageable budget, the P3C is a great place to start.

Works with multiple materials and nozzle sizes in the same print

Why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Bambu Lab didn’t even tease the arrival of the new P3C, a smaller, more budget-friendly version of the H3C, which retails at roughly half the price. In fact, this post might be the first time you’ve heard more than just a rumor about the tool changer’s mysterious little brother.

The Bambu Lab P3C combo is a tool changer with room for seven tools and a 256 x 256 x 260mm build volume, roughly the same as the P2S. It ships as either a five-tool unit, with two empty slots for later customization, or as a seven-tool “multi-material combo” with six 1.75mm tools and one 2.85mm tool. Bambu is bringing back old school 2.85mm filament in the form of super squishy TPU 75A.

The five-tool unit is priced at $1,149, while the seven-tool is launching at $1,299.

It offers the same excellent TPU printing process for both standard and phat TPU and has quickly joined the select group of send it and forget it printers in my fleet. I’ve had very few failures, even when printing more technical filaments.

The P3C is not quite as tall as the H3C, but it does require almost 4ft (1,212 mm) of vertical space for the AMS lid to fully open. So plan accordingly and have a good space picked out in advance.

Bambu’s most annoying cost-saving measure took the A right out of AMS. There’s no motor of any sort in the AMS 3P, leaving you to manually load and unload the filament all the way to the nozzle. The process takes a long time if you are loading all of the filament slots. The upside of not having powered rollers is that the AMS 3P will run almost any 1kg or smaller spool without issue.

The printer can run different-sized nozzles from .2 mm to .8 mm, and has an optional 2.85 mm TPU filament tool. The FlexFeed extruder with Active Grip Control just pushes whatever filament it’s asked to while changing on the fly. It may be the best extruder I’ve reviewed, however, the printer as a whole is not quite what we need for the best 3D printers of 2026.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

413 x 538 x 925 mm (16.25 x 21.18 x 36.4 in)

The Bambu Lab P3C comes with five .4mm tools preinstalled in the bottom of the AMS 3P. Also included are a toolkit and cables needed to assemble the printer, along with quick start guides for both the printer and AMS 3P, and a few spare parts. It does not come with a USB memory stick, which is needed for recording time lapses.

We received the multi-material combo for review, which came with five tools installed, plus two additional tools I had to set up myself (one 1.75mm and one 2.85mm), along with several spools of PLA Palette and 2.85mm TPU 75A.

The P3C is missing several perks of the bigger H3C in order to save costs and keep the price reasonable. The most disappointing is the lack of a motor to drive the filament spools. This makes the “A” in the AMS 3P questionable, as you are forced to manually feed the filament all the way to the nozzle, as well as handle retraction when unloading.

The AMS 3P also does not come with a filament drier, although an optional 75C dryer will be available for $159.90.

The basic Bambu Lab P3C comes standard with only five tools and is expandable to seven. The Swaptek system keeps the cooling fans and extruder on the toolhead, with each tool having its own filament path, heater, and a hardened steel nozzle. When printing, the idle tools are preheated, allowing for extremely fast tool swaps.

The nozzles on each tool can be swapped out with different sizes, and multiple sizes can be used in the same print.

Bambu Lab will also release tools for cutting, drawing, debossing, and foil transfer in the future.

The Bambu Lab P3C supports printing TPU with a bypass port on all filament slots except 2 and 6, which allows TPU to skip the tube, reducing friction. If you have the optional 2.85mm tool, you can mount it to any slot with a bypass.

Please note that the 2.85mm tool has a wider filament path – it's not just the nozzle tip that changes dimensions.

The tools dock on a rack in front of the printer which retracts after each tool change, allowing for a clear view of the build plate.

The Flexfeed extruder is impressive. It switches from 1.75mm to 2.85mm filament on the fly and uses what Bambu Lab calls Active Grip Control with feedback from the extruder motor.

Like the H3C, there are magnetic covers on the left and right sides of the AMS and a front cover that attaches in slots to allow easy access to the chamber for maintenance. The front cover is a bit tricky, and you need to lift the AMS up to get it free. For this reason, I didn’t bother to secure the AMS to the base of the printer. You really need to remove that front panel to change out the tools.

Changing tools is one of the few frustrating things about the Bambu Lab P3C (or the H3C, as it’s the same process). There is very little room to work, and there are sharp plastic edges that left me bloodied on one occasion. I would suggest picking your favorite configuration and leaving it there if you can.

The AMS is massive and requires a lot of additional vertical space to fully open the lid to get at the spools. Bambu Lab recommends a clearance of 1,212 mm or almost four feet from the base in order to open the lid. Surprisingly, this smaller P3C is only 3.58 inches shorter than the big H3C. With the printer sitting on a standard countertop, a step-stool will be mandatory equipment for most people. Bambu offers a rolling cart for the H3C that puts the printer at a more manageable height, and I would highly recommend getting it for the P3C.

The base unit of the Bambu Lab P3C looks similar to the P and X series printers, with a plastic outer frame and a steel chassis. The build plate is a standard 256 x 256 mm, with 260 mm available on the Z-axis. The P3C does not have active chamber heating, but being enclosed with a max of 300C on the nozzle and 110C on the bed, it has the ability to print many of the more common technical filaments. The chamber is ventilated with HEPA and active carbon filtration.

The 3D printer has a great camera, which is used for AI detection and monitoring using the Bambu Handy app and the device page of Bambu Slicer. The camera can produce time-lapses of your prints but does require a USB memory stick to store them.

The Bambu Lab P3C and AMS 3P ship in separate boxes but are almost fully assembled. After removing the packaging, there are two screws holding the dock retainers that need to be removed and 6 screws securing the bed in place.

There is a helpful reminder to do this when the printer is first turned on. AMS 3P is mounted on top of the printer and requires a good deal of vertical space. There are four screws to attach the AMS 3P to the printer, but I left these off since the front panel of the AMS is easier to remove when you can tip the AMS back a little.

The individual tools attach to the dock magnetically and must be placed manually, which can take a little fiddling to get used to.

The touch screen attaches to the front of the printer without tools, and the ribbon cable to connect it is just long enough to work.

The Bambu Lab P3C levels its bed as part of its initial calibration and again at the start of every print. The system works perfectly.

The Bambu Lab P3C does not have auto-loading, as there is no motor.

When loading multiple new filaments for a print, the process can take a while and is very hands-on. When using normal 1.75 mm filament, the material is pushed into the orange tube in the AMS when called for by the printer.

When using TPU, either 1.75mm or 2.85 filament, drop the filament into a slot with a bypass port in the bottom and drag it by hand to the tool. The normal Bowden tube must be removed from the tool and clipped to the side. When running 1.75mm TPU a short piece of bowden tube must be inserted into the tool to help feed the filament correctly. The 2.85mm TPU doesn’t need the short tube and can feed directly.

The printer has a helpful filament guide to walk you through the loading operation.

Bambu Lab-branded filament with RFID tags will automatically enter the filament type and color. Other brands must be entered manually via the printer’s touchscreen.

Unloading filament is the reverse of loading. You’ll need to manually retract material once it is cut by the printer. There is a batch unloading command that will allow you to wait until all of the selected filaments have been cut.

Bambu Studio is based on PrusaSlicer and its predecessors. New for the P3C and the H3C is the ability to mix different tool sizes. It is one of the best slicers available with good filament mapping, control and print monitoring, with access to Makerworld, Bambu Lab’s file sharing service.

The P3C does not come with filament samples. Bambu Lab sent a few spools of their new PLA Palette and 2.85mm 75A TPU to try. Be sure to check out our best filaments for 3D printing to fill up your AMS 3P.

This print of Carl and Donut from the Dungeon Crawler Carl book series took 15 hours and 35 minutes to print using a .16mm layer height for smooth detail. I used the default settings, but slowed the outer walls to 65mm/s. The print is exceptionally good, though the supports left a few marks under horizontal areas like the arms and shin. Normally I’d tilt a model this back 45 degrees to save time and support, but the fin on this particular model is vexing and would have added an hour to the print time and another 10g of support.

This is printed in seven colors of PLA, maxing out the P3C slots. Polymaker HT-PLA Pro White, Prusament Galaxy Black and Galaxy Silver PLA, Elegoo PLA Brown and Silk Red, Inland Bone White, and Matterhacker’s Purple MH Build Series PLA.

Printing with seven colors allows you more creative freedom when printing complex models. Though the brown did a lot of heavy lifting on this print, I think the P3C really captured Carl nicely.

I tried some of Bambu Lab’s matte PETG on a Cute Blue Jay from Makerworld. Since the model prints best straight up and down, and requires pretty extensive supports, I used a scrap of Prusa Lipstick Red PLA as an interface layer.

Using a .16mm layer height, the print took 8 hours and 55 minutes running at a little under 100mm/s on average. The matte PETG makes the model look like it was painted. This is printed in black, white and baby blue matte PETG and the supports came off with no residue what so ever.

Though the P3C doesn’t get hot enough to print PPS, it does print most PA, PC, and PET filaments very well. I printed a spool and a half of Sunlu Easy PA, making all of the mechanical parts for two radio-controlled Death Racers. Initially, I made just a few items per plate, but with just a little glue stick, the bed adhesion was so good that I felt comfortable loading up the plates as full as possible and had zero failures. All were printed with a .2mm layer height and slowed to 100mm/s by me in the slicer. Other than a tiny bit of stringing, the parts are perfect mechanically.

The Bambu Lab P3C’s HEPA filter does a good job filtering the stinkier filaments like ABS and ASA. I printed this wire holding vice using Fusion ABS matte ionized cobalt black and Prusa lipstick red ASA.

This is printed with a .2 mm layer height and an average print speed of 120mm/s. The entire print took a little less than 2 hours and 3 minutes, and the parts fit together perfectly.

With the H3C and now the P3C, I have seen the future of printing with TPU. The AMS 3P bypass ports are just the ticket for printing soft materials.

I printed several plates of treads for my RC Death Racer project. Normally, I print these a few at a time to limit the fallout from print failures, but this proved unnecessary. I ran 48 treads in Bambu Lab Cyan 2.85mm TPU 75A and another 48 using Bambu Lab 90A TPU. Both prints used a .2mm layer height and were limited to 100 mm/s in the slicer. The 75A print finished a little quicker at 19 hours 10 minutes, with the 90A filament taking 19 hours and 40 minutes.

Both are terrific prints with no stringing at all and zero failures.

The P3C can print almost any filament I own beautifully. It lacks a few creature comforts like auto-loading, filament drying (which can be upgraded), and a heated chamber. It’s also tall enough to require a step stool to load those back filament slots.

The Bambu Lab P3C is best for anyone who wants poop-free multicolor, multi-material printing without paying H3C money. I highly recommend it for anyone who plans to print a lot of TPU and doesn’t need that larger build plate. If you can live without the automatic feeding you normally get from a Bambu printer, then the money you’ll save in filament is worth the hassle.

This machine gives you most of the advantages of the Bambu Lab H3C at roughly half the $2,499 price tag. The open-source four-color Snapmaker U1 is still worth it right now while it’s on sale for $699. Another option is the Creality K3, which is another four-color tool changer with a similar build size for $849.

Denise Bertacchi is a Contributing Writer for Tom’s Hardware US, covering 3D printing. Denise has been crafting with PCs since she discovered Print Shop had clip art on her Apple IIe. She loves reviewing 3D printers because she can mix all her passions: printing, photography, and writing.

#10296. Why Donald Trump Jr.’s investment firm is the focus of a widening probe in the House

A top House Democrat is broadening his investigation into Donald Trump Jr.’s venture capital fund 1789 Capital by demanding records from four companies that secured an investment before benefiting from lucrative federal contracts or policies.

Rep. Jamie Raskin, the ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee and the panel’s incoming chair, sent letters on Monday evening to the defense contractor Hadrian Automation, vape maker Juul Labs, prediction market platform Polymarket and the online firearms seller GrabAGun.

The Maryland congressman requested that each firm send him two years’ worth of communications with 1789 Capital and other select documents, saying the materials would help him investigate whether U.S. President Donald Trump’s eldest son used insider information to orchestrate or anticipate government actions that boosted the companies and his own finances.

The investigation was opened over the summer

Both Trump Jr. and 1789 Capital, which is based in Palm Beach, Florida, deny any wrongdoing.

The letters ramp up an investigation that Raskin opened in August into Trump Jr.’s firm, which he said “suddenly struck investment gold” after naming the president’s son as a partner in 2024. As one of the lawmakers who will be spearheading Democrats’ oversight of the Trump administration when they take control of Congress in January, Raskin has said that uncovering information about bribery and financial corruption will be among his top priorities.

Trump Jr. has repeatedly rejected accusations that he has exploited government access for profit. At an Axios event last week, he acknowledged that he understood people’s corruption concerns, but said that they weren’t accurate, noting he has been an investor for decades.

“I can see what they are saying. It doesn’t make it so,” he said. “The notion that I should somehow sit in a corner, suck my thumb and wait, you know, eight years — in this case 12 years — till we’re out of the political game, it’s not real.”

Trump Jr. and the firm deny any wrongdoing

1789 Capital also has forcefully denied claims of wrongdoing. In a letter to Raskin in September, the company’s lawyers defended the firm’s investment thesis as predating Trump’s administration and said that while it “welcomes legitimate congressional oversight,” it “has no intention of being held hostage to political gamesmanship.”

On Monday, the company’s attorney, Bill Burck, said the September letter explained flaws in Raskin’s understanding, but Raskin “never bothered to reply.”

“Facts are facts and Congressman Raskin has them wrong here, but persists in his tall tales against 1789,” Burck said. “These are personal attacks untethered to actual evidence.”

‘Serendipitous timing’ of investments, Raskin says in letters

The firm was founded in 2022 and Trump Jr. was announced as a partner in November 2024.

In his letters to the four companies obtained by The Associated Press, Raskin outlined how federal policies or contracts had benefited their businesses and claimed that 1789 Capital had suspiciously “serendipitous timing” when it invested in them.

Hadrian Automation, he wrote, received nearly $1 billion in U.S. Navy and Army contracts in March — its first-ever federal contracts — after bringing 1789 Capital on as an investor in 2025.

Juul, Raskin wrote, received Food and Drug Administration clearance to keep its electronic cigarette products on the market in July 2025, four months after 1789 Capital had taken a stake in the company.

The congressman wrote that GrabAGun got help from 1789 to go public and put Trump Jr. on its board before the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives issued a proposed rule to ease the process of shipping guns to people’s homes.

Raskin calls Trump administration order ‘blatantly unlawful’

Raskin also raised questions about the Justice Department and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission closing investigations into Polymarket in July 2025, after 1789 Capital already had invested in the prediction market platform.
GrabAGun said in a statement that Raskin’s letter “is a political document, and its allegations are baseless.”

“ATF’s review of its regulations was well known across the firearms industry, and the agency published numerous proposed rules for public comment. GrabAGun’s only input came through public comments on several of those proposals,” the statement read.

Juul Labs said that it was reviewing its letter closely.

“As always, we intend to cooperate with any Congressional effort to understand our company, our commitment to combating underage vaping, and our mission to help adult smokers of combustible cigarettes transition completely away from smoking,” it said in an emailed response.

The other recipients of the letters didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

The Trump administration has taken steps to push back on the Democrats’ oversight efforts, including an executive order on Friday directing federal contractors and subcontractors to consult with his administration about inquiries they receive from Congress and to withhold any communications that the White House considers privileged.

That could complicate compliance with Raskin’s investigation for at least one of the companies, Hadrian Automation, which is a federal contractor.

Raskin has called Trump’s order “blatantly unlawful” and said that public contractors have a “duty and a right to speak truthfully when Congress calls.”

—Ali Swenson, Associated Press

#10295. How Much Latency Does a Self-Hosted LLM Gateway Add? Langfuse vs LiteLLM vs AcruxCore

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A self-hosted LLM gateway sits between your app and the model provider, so every call pays for one extra hop. We measured that cost for three open-source gateways: the Langfuse AI Gateway, the LiteLLM proxy and AcruxCore. Each one ran on the same machine, in front of the same OpenAI model. LiteLLM added 61 to 67 ms to every non-streaming call. AcruxCore added 15 to 24 ms. Langfuse's number could not be told apart from zero.

The bigger lesson was about the measurement itself. Before we controlled for it, one OpenAI network address moved our results by more than any gateway did.

Each number is the median time a gateway added to a direct OpenAI call, with its 95% interval in brackets. A gateway can log each call, and logging takes time, so we ran the test three times with three logging levels.

The direct call took 781 to 831 ms at the median, so even LiteLLM's cost is under 9% of a short call. Read the tables this way:

The obvious test is to time 100 calls through the gateway, time 100 direct calls, and compare the two medians. That test gives the wrong answer, for two reasons.

The first reason is noise. OpenAI's own response time moved by hundreds of milliseconds between calls in our runs. The direct call's p95 was 1,047 to 1,233 ms against a median near 800 ms. A gateway that adds 20 ms is hidden inside that spread unless the test removes it.

The second reason is the network path to OpenAI. It does not stay the same between a direct client and a gateway, and that difference can be larger than the gateway itself.

api.openai.com resolves to more than one address. From our network, DNS returned two Cloudflare addresses, and one was much farther away than the other. We measured both with a script that pins one address at a time:

On a connection that is already open, both addresses answer in the same time. On a new connection, the far address adds about 250 ms, because the TCP and TLS handshakes take that much longer.

A gateway keeps its connection to OpenAI open between calls. It pays the setup once and then stays on whichever address it reached first. A client that opens a new connection for each call pays the setup again on every call. How much it pays depends on which address DNS returns that time.

Node's built-in fetch closes an idle connection after about 4 seconds. So a test client that calls OpenAI every few seconds reconnects on almost every call. In our first, uncontrolled run, the Langfuse gateway came out 43 ms faster than calling OpenAI directly. A gateway cannot be faster than the call it forwards. The direct client paid for new connections, and the gateway did not.

The fix has two parts. First, pin api.openai.com to one address on every path. In Docker, that is an extra_hosts entry on each gateway container:

Second, let the direct client keep its connection open, as a gateway does. With undici, the HTTP client behind Node's fetch, that is a custom Agent:

We then listed each container's open connections to confirm that every path used the same address. The edge-check script is in the repository linked at the end, and it takes about a minute to run from your own network.

This advice also applies outside benchmarks. If your app calls OpenAI directly from Node, keep the connection open between calls. Otherwise some of your calls pay the handshake, and on a far address that costs about 250 ms.

Each test sent 150 rounds after 5 warm-up rounds. One round calls OpenAI directly and through each gateway, once without streaming and once with streaming. The order rotates every round, so no path always goes first or last.

For each round, the script takes the gateway's time minus the direct call's time in that same round. Calls in one round are made within a few seconds of each other, so a slow moment at OpenAI hits all four paths together and cancels out of the difference. The script then reports the median of the 150 differences.

The interval comes from a bootstrap. The script draws 150 differences at random, with replacement, and takes their median. It repeats that 2,000 times, and the middle 95% of those medians is the interval. This is a shortened version of the script's function:

An interval that includes zero means the test could not separate the gateway's cost from zero. That is what the Langfuse rows show. It does not prove that the cost is zero.

Every call used OpenAI gpt-6-luna with reasoning_effort: "none", the same short prompt and a cap of 5 output tokens. A short answer keeps the model's own time small, so more of the measured time belongs to the path. Each streamed call measured the time to its first token. Each non-streamed call measured the time to the full response.

All three gateways did real work on every call, which made the comparison fair:

The three logging levels mapped to these settings:

The machine was an AMD Ryzen 9 5900X with 62 GB of RAM, running Fedora Linux and Docker 29.9. All three stacks ran on it at once, and the test was run on 10 November 2026.

LiteLLM added 61 to 67 ms to the full response, but only 9 to 43 ms to the first streamed token. The first token arrives as soon as the model starts to answer, so time spent before that point shows up in both numbers. The larger cost without streaming suggests that most of LiteLLM's extra time is spent after the model has answered. We did not profile LiteLLM to confirm this.

Logging level made no clear difference for any gateway. Adding LiteLLM's Langfuse callback did not raise its cost. AcruxCore's median rose from 15 ms with logging off to 24 ms with full logging, but its intervals overlap across all three runs. AcruxCore's median is 16 to 24 ms above Langfuse's, and those intervals overlap too, so this test does not rank the two of them.

If 60 ms per call matters to you, as in a chat app that makes several model calls per user message, LiteLLM's cost is real and repeatable. Langfuse and AcruxCore stayed near or within the noise. If your calls take several seconds, any of the three costs less than OpenAI's own variation from one call to the next.

Before you trust a gateway number, your own or anyone else's, check two things. Was each gateway compared with a direct call in the same round? And did the direct client keep its connection open on the same OpenAI address as the gateway? Without both, the result measures the network path and not the gateway.

The scripts, Compose files and raw results are on GitHub: scripts/comparison/langfuse-gateway-vs-litellm-vs-acruxcore.

Talha Anwar is a senior AI and full-stack engineer and writes about building and running AI systems.

#10291. Google broke its biggest promise about Gmail. It’s the one thing no company should ever do

Promises, by their very nature, are inconvenient. You tell someone you’re going to do something, and then you have to do it. Or, you promise you’ll never do something, and now you’ve restricted your options.

Of course, the benefit of all that inconvenience is that people trust you when you keep your promises. And trust, as I’ve written before, is your most valuable asset, especially when you’re a massive company whose entire business depends on the willingness of your customers to give you their personal information. Like Google.

Which is why it was such a big deal back in 2017 when Google promised it would not scan your Gmail in order to show you personalized ads. Previously, Google would scan your email to decide which ads to show. People didn’t love that, so Google told customers their data was their own and wouldn’t be used for ads.

For almost a decade, that was the deal. You could use Gmail, Google Photos, and Google Drive without worrying that the information you stored in those services would be used as a source of ad recommendations.

Earlier this month, however, the company quietly updated its privacy policy to say that it would use information from Gmail, Google Photos, and Google Drive to influence the ads people see. Specifically, the policy—which took effect October 16—says that information from those services can be used to personalize advertisements when users choose to connect them to other Google products that have personalized advertising.

The most obvious reason Google is doing this is Personal Intelligence, which lets users connect their Gmail, Search, and Photos to Gemini. The reason you might want to do this is that it turns out that AI can be very useful at pulling information from your email, for example. Of course, that’s very different from wanting Google to then show you ads based on what it finds.

To be clear, it’s not that Google is suddenly scanning everyone’s inbox to sell ads. You have to turn on the connection—it’s off by default. In addition, Google isn’t giving your personal information to advertisers, and it says it doesn’t directly target ads based on the data you have in those services. Instead, Google’s AI can use information derived from connected apps to personalize ads.

I’m sure there’s some kind of technical distinction there, but I don’t know that it’s all that meaningful if you’re someone who has trusted Google with all your information. Say, for example, you are planning a trip, and you ask Gemini to help you plan activities when you’re there. You give it access to your email so it can find your flights and then track whether the price changes.

That’s super useful, and it’s the kind of thing that AI tools are actually really good at. Imagine, however, if suddenly you started seeing ads for things to do near your travel destination. Under Google’s new policy, information derived from that reservation could definitely influence the advertisements you see.

Look, it’s not that Google is doing something inherently wrong. You can certainly decide for yourself whether you want to connect your accounts at all. Also, to its credit, Google is disclosing how that information might be used. The problem is that Google is changing the terms of a promise it made in order to earn people’s trust in the first place. And you can’t connect Personal Intelligence and take advantage of its genuine benefits without opting in to the ad part.

Every company eventually faces a situation where keeping a promise it made to its users suddenly becomes inconvenient. Maybe it’s because the market changes, or because its competitors introduce something new, or there’s an opportunity to make more money.

When that happens, it’s tempting to find a technical reason for changing the terms of the deal. Google could reasonably argue that its new policy is different from its old practice because users have to opt in and their emails aren’t directly used to select advertisements. But you don’t build trust with technical distinctions in your privacy policy. You build it by being clear about what customers can expect, and then doing exactly that.

In Google’s case, the promise was simple: We won’t use the information you put in Gmail to personalize advertising. Now, if you want to connect your personal information to Google’s AI product, it will.

The most important thing a company can do is keep its promises, especially when doing so becomes inconvenient. The worst thing that can happen is that customers start wondering which promises you’ll keep and which ones you’ll change when you see a better business opportunity. Once that happens, you’ve already lost something far more valuable than whatever you hoped to gain.

—Jason Aten

This article originally appeared on Fast Company’s sister website, Inc.com.

#10290. Leaders: transformation should not be your focus

In his 1980 book Managing in Turbulent Times, management guru Peter Drucker wrote, “The greatest danger in times of turbulence is not the turbulence; it is to act with yesterday’s logic.” This seems obvious. But more often than not, businesses lean into safe, tried and true, old-school thinking as their life raft during uncertain times. Consider Nvidia, initially defending keeping Jensen Huang in place as CEO amidst accusations of major ethical missteps. 

It may be tempting to think that the other side of turbulence is overhauling the organization in a major transformation effort. But Geoff Tuff and Steve Goldbach, who are leaders in Deloitte’s sustainability practice, have a different take on moving through organizational turbulence. They believe that large-scale transformation is not the right focus. In fact, their research and experience show that organizations who focus on transformation tend to fail. 

What they offer instead is an alternative view that is compellingly explored in their book Hone: How Purposeful Leaders Defy Drift. Cumulatively, Geoff and Steve have decades of experience working with Fortune 500 companies that end up drifting in the process of trying to transform. When I recently spoke with them they shared that “drift” is the unintentional, imperceptible shift that leaves an organization uncompetitive because leaders fail to make micro-adjustments along the way. The solution? Hone: make small, intentional continuous adjustments to stay on course rather than wait until a massive disruption is necessary.

Here are my three biggest takeaways from our conversation.

1. Honing is the antidote to failed transformation. Broad-scale transformations carry a 70% failure rate because humans naturally resist drastic change. This leads to organizational “tissue rejection.” Instead replace massive transformation with continuous “honing” to prevent drift. Geoff’s pastime and love of sailing have clearly influenced their perspective. Because just like adjusting a boat’s autopilot to account for winds and currents, leaders should focus on honing (for example, micro-adjustments in leadership style, accountability, KPI’s, etc.)  to stay on course rather than wait until a massive, disruptive transformation is required.

2. AI can help identify where honing is needed. Invisible drift can be made visible because AI can detect subtle patterns and organizational drift that are otherwise invisible to the human eye, enabling managers to address issues proactively. An AI enabled organizational network analysis can track thousands of interactions over time (such as email and Slack messages about meetings). For example, it can spot if an engineering team’s contact with the product team has decreased over 30% over multiple quarters. A 2021 study published in Nature Human Behaviour showed that a 60,000 person Microsoft team’s collaboration efforts decreased when the team went remote. Employees engaged in more intra-team communication than inter-team communication. AI can serve as an early warning system, surface weak signals and alert leaders about a future they may not want so that they can course correct. 

3. Honing demands deep behavioral curiosity. The good news is that we can adopt a “honing mindset.” A successful “honer” walks through the world constructively dissatisfied with current processes. And not because they’re unhappy, but because they’re more critically curious and attuned to identify design flaws, eliminate waste, and continuously tweak systems. Organizations change when the individuals within them start behaving differently. To drive that change, leaders must practice self-awareness and empathy to understand what truly motivates their teams.

If you’re wondering how to make honing a regular behavioral practice on your own team, start by inviting someone in from the outside. It should be a person from a different team or even a different industry who can cast a bird’s eye view on your operations and ask the “naive questions.” In design thinking we call this “lateral thinking.” Then, collect three of their questions and keep them as regular trackers that you continuously go back to asking yourself and your team as navigational tools. Because just as it’s easier to spot a ship that’s going off course from the shoreline, an outsider can help spark the necessary micro-adjustments to ensure that you’re honing- not drifting.
